chapters: God made the heavens and the earth; the earth was void, unfilled / Darkness lay on the deep; God’s Spirit hovered o’er waters there
God said, “Let there be light,” and light appeared in sight / He split it from the dark, named day and night outright
God spread an expanse, with waters below and waters high / He named that broad dividing expanse the open sky
God gathered waters under sky; dry land came to be / He named the land Earth, and called the gathered waters seas
God said, “Let earth yield grass, seed-bearing herbs, and fruit trees” / The earth brought forth each kind of herb and tree with seeds
God set lights in the sky, dividing night from day / Their signs mark seasons, days, and years along the way
The greater light ruled day; the lesser ruled the night / He set the stars in the sky to give the earth light
God made great sea creatures and all that swim below / He made each winged bird, each kind, to fly above
God blessed sea creatures and birds: “Be fruitful,” He said / Fill the waters in the seas; let birds multiply on earth, He said
God told earth, “Bring livestock, creeping things across the land” / He made each kind of land beast by His own command
God said, “Let’s make man in our image and likeness too” / “Let them rule fish, birds, livestock, all earth, and what moves”
God made mankind in His own image, male and female / There was evening, there was morning; the sixth day reached its span
God blessed them: “Be fruitful; multiply; fill it all” / “Subdue it; rule fish, birds, beasts, and all creatures that crawl”
He gave mankind seed-bearing plants and fruit trees for food / Green herbs for beasts, birds, crawlers; all was very good
God finished heaven and earth, rested on the seventh day / He blessed it, made it holy, put his work away
Before the plants had sprung, mist watered all the ground / No man was there to till the soil; no tiller could be found
God formed the man from dust of ground, breathed life through his nose / And man became a living soul; new life in him arose
God planted Eden’s garden, trees for sight and food / The tree of life, the good-and-evil knowledge tree, stood
God placed the man in Eden’s garden, set him there / To cultivate and keep it, entrusted to his care
God said, “From every garden tree, you may freely eat / But don’t eat the knowledge tree; that day you’ll surely die.”
God said, “It is not good for man to live apart / I’ll make a helper suited to him, his counterpart.”
God brought the birds and beasts; the man named every one / No helper comparable was found; there was none
God put the man in deep sleep; from him took one rib / He closed the flesh, made woman, brought her to him
“Bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh,” said the man / He called her Woman, for from Man she began
A man leaves his parents, joins his wife; they unite / They are one flesh, both naked, with no shame in sight
The serpent asked, “Did God forbid fruit from each garden tree?” / She said, “We eat from all but one; don’t touch or eat, or die.”
The snake said, “You won’t die; your eyes will open wide,” / “You’ll be like God, know good and evil,” he replied.
She took some fruit and ate, then gave her husband his share; / Her husband ate it too, with her beside him there.
Their eyes were opened, and they knew that they both were bare, / They stitched fig leaves together, made coverings to wear.
They heard Yahweh God walking and hid themselves away; / God called to the man, “Where are you?” in the cool of day.
Who told you that you were naked? Did you eat the tree I forbade? / I feared, naked, hid; the woman you gave me gave fruit; I ate.
The woman told God, “The serpent deceived me,” / “I ate the fruit that grew upon the garden tree.”
God cursed the snake; eat dust; strife between them they'd feel; / Her seed and his: “He’ll bruise your head; you’ll bruise his heel.”
Pain in childbirth; desire for your husband; he rules your days; / The ground is cursed; you’ll sweat for bread all your days till dust takes you away.
God clothed them in skins; Adam named Eve, all living’s mother, his wife; / Like God, he knows good and evil; lest he eat the tree of life.
God sent him out of Eden to till the cursed ground; / Cherubim and a flaming sword guarded the way around.
Eve bore Cain: “With Yahweh’s help, I got a man.” / Then Eve bore Abel, who kept sheep; Cain tilled the land.
Cain brought produce from the ground; Yahweh chose to reject. / Abel’s firstborn flock and fat Yahweh did accept.
Cain grew angry; his face fell; sin crouched there by the door. / Yahweh said, “If you do well, rise; sin seeks you—rule it there.”
Cain said to Abel, “Let’s go into the field”; they were there. / There Cain rose against his own brother and left Abel dead.
Yahweh asked Cain where Abel was; “I don’t know,” he said. / “Am I my brother’s keeper?” Cain answered instead.
Yahweh said Abel’s blood cried out from the ground. / “The ground won’t yield its strength; you’ll flee and wander around.”
Cain said, “My punishment is more than I can bear.” / “Whoever finds me will kill me,” he declared.
Yahweh said Cain’s killer would pay seven times in kind. / He set a sign to guard him; Cain left Yahweh’s presence behind.
Cain lived in Nod; his son Enoch was born. / He built a city, Enoch’s name it would adorn.
From Cain’s line, through generations, Lamech was known. / He took two wives, Adah and Zillah, as his own.
Lamech told his wives, “I killed a man for wounding me.” / “If Cain’s avenged sevenfold, seventy-sevenfold I’ll be.”
Adam and Eve had Seth in Abel’s place, their son. / When Enosh was born, calling Yahweh’s name had begun.
God made them in His likeness, blessed male and female that day / On their creation day, He named them Adam, Scripture says
At one-thirty, Seth was born, Adam’s likeness passed along / Then other sons and daughters came; eight hundred years rolled on
Adam lived nine hundred thirty years, his life was long / Then Adam, he died, and all of his days were gone
At one-oh-five, Seth fathered Enosh, the next in line / More sons and daughters; nine-twelve marked the end of his time
At ninety, Enosh fathered Kenan, and his line then grew / More sons and daughters; at nine-oh-five, his life was then through
At seventy, Kenan fathered Mahalalel, his son / More sons and daughters; nine-ten years, his life was then done
At sixty-five, Mahalalel fathered Jared, his son / More sons and daughters; eight-ninety-five years, then life was done
At one-sixty-two, Jared fathered Enoch, his son / More sons and daughters; nine-sixty-two, he died there
At sixty-five, Enoch fathered Methuselah, his son / Then walked with God three hundred years; more sons and daughters born
Enoch lived three hundred sixty-five years, as records say / He was not found, for God had then taken him away
One-eighty-seven, Methuselah fathered Lamech, his son / More sons and daughters; nine-sixty-nine, his life was then done
At one-eighty-two, Lamech fathered Noah, named him at birth / He will comfort us in work and our hand-toil from Yahweh-cursed earth
Lamech died at seven-seventy-seven; his life was done / At five hundred, Noah fathered sons: Shem, Ham, Japheth, one by one
Men multiplied on earth; their daughters came to be / God’s sons saw they were beautiful, took wives as they’d please
Yahweh said, “My Spirit won’t strive with man forevermore” / “For he is flesh; his days are one hundred twenty years, no more”
The Nephilim were on earth then, and after that again / God’s sons came in to men’s daughters; mighty, famed men
Yahweh saw each thought was only evil, grieved he’d made mankind / He’d destroy humans, animals, birds, and creeping things of each kind
Noah found favor, righteous, blameless in his time / He walked with God; Shem, Ham, Japheth, his sons in line
The earth was corrupt before God, violence filled the land / God told Noah all flesh and earth would end at his command
Build gopher-wood ship, rooms, pitch sealed inside and outside / Three hundred long, fifty wide, thirty high; roof, side door, three levels
God would send floodwaters; all flesh beneath the sky would die / He’d covenant with Noah; his household would board and survive
Bring two of every kind aboard; gather food for them and you / Noah did everything that God had commanded him to do
Yahweh said, “Come, Noah, with your household; board the ship, and go; / Your righteousness before me in this generation I know.”
Yahweh: “Take seven pairs: clean beasts; seven pairs birds, male with mate; / One pair of each unclean kind, with male and female paired.”
“In seven days, I’ll send forty days and nights of rain, / And destroy every living thing I made from the terrain.”
Noah did everything Yahweh commanded him to do; / He was six hundred when the floodwaters came through.
Noah went in with sons, wife, sons’ wives with him; / Because of floodwaters, they entered the ship.
All of the kinds went in, male and female within; / As God had commanded him, Yahweh shut Noah in.
The deep fountains burst; the sky’s windows poured rain down, / For forty days and nights, the rain fell on the ground.
Waters rose and lifted up the ship on high; / It floated on the waters beneath the sky.
Every high mountain under the sky was covered by flow; / The waters rose fifteen cubits higher than peaks below.
All of the flesh—man, birds, livestock, crawlers—died; / All breath-filled beings on dry land, none survived.
Only Noah and those with him alive remained; / Waters covered earth; a hundred fifty days reigned.
God remembered Noah and all who were aboard / He sent a wind; rain ceased, floodwaters were lowered
Noah, he sent a raven out over the plain / It went back and forth till the waters were drained
The dove found no place to rest and returned to him / He put out his hand, took her, and brought her within
At evening, olive leaf; the waters receded more / Seven days later he sent her; she returned nevermore
Noah removed the covering; dry land met his eye / By the second month’s twenty-seventh day, earth was dry
God told Noah, “You and your family, leave the ship and go” / “Bring every living creature out; breed and multiply and grow”
Noah and his family went out, left the ship behind / Each beast, bird, creeping thing followed outside
Noah built an altar to Yahweh; burnt offerings he made / Each clean beast and bird upon the altar he laid
Yahweh smelled the pleasant aroma; he’d not curse ground once more / For man's heart's evil from youth; nor strike all living things as before
Seedtime and harvest keep on returning each year / Cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night reappear
God blessed Noah and his sons: be fruitful, fill the land / All beasts, birds, fish were placed beneath their hand
All moving life is food; its blood you shall not eat / I’ll call beasts and men to account for human blood they reap
Whoever sheds a man’s blood, his blood by man will run / For God made humankind in His image, each one
God covenants with Noah, his seed, all living kind / No flood to cut off flesh again, nor earth-destroying tide
God sets his rainbow in the clouds, the covenant’s sign / When it appears, he remembers the covenant each time
The sons of Noah were Shem, Ham, and Japheth, all three / The whole earth was populated from these
Noah then became a farmer, working the ground / He planted a vineyard, rows of vines all around
Noah drank the wine and he grew drunk within his tent / He was uncovered there, his nakedness evident
Ham saw his own father naked, then he spoke / To both his brothers outside; the news he broke
Garment on their shoulders, Shem and Japheth faced the rear / They went in backward, covered him, and did not see
Noah awoke from wine and knew what his youngest had done / He cursed Canaan: servant of servants to brothers, each one
Noah blessed Yahweh, Shem’s God; Canaan serve; Japheth grow wide / Noah lived three-fifty years after the flood, then died
Noah’s sons all had descendants after the flood / Shem, Ham, and Japheth’s families sprang from that blood
Japheth’s descendants became nations across lands / Their families and languages divided those clans
Ham, he had fathered four sons, whose names were proclaimed / Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan, they were all named
Cush fathered Nimrod, a mighty one on earth, made clear / “Like Nimrod, mighty hunter before Yahweh”—the saying is heard
In Shinar, Nimrod’s kingdom began at Babel / Erech, Accad, and Calneh completed the table
From Shinar he went into Assyria’s wide domain / Built Nineveh, Rehoboth Ir, Calah, Resen in terrain
Mizraim fathered many peoples, their names the text displays / From Casluhim Philistines descended, as the record says
Canaan fathered Sidon, Heth, and many a clan / His descendants formed a wide ancestral span
Afterward the Canaanite families spread out / From Sidon toward Lasha their border traced a route
Shem, elder brother of Japheth, Eber’s line is shown / Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, and Aram are known
Through Arpachshad, Shelah, Eber, the lineage grew / Peleg and Joktan born; in Peleg’s days, earth split in two
Joktan fathered descendants, their names in array / Their dwelling stretched from Mesha toward Sephar away
The whole earth shared one language, and one speech rang clear / From the east they found Shinar’s plain and they settled there
They burned bricks thoroughly; brick stood in place of stone / Tar served as mortar, binding all the bricks as one
They planned a city, tower reaching to the sky / They sought a name, lest they be scattered far and wide
Yahweh came down to see the work that they had made / The city and the tower stood before his gaze
Yahweh said: one people, one language combined / Nothing they intend to do would be denied
Yahweh said, “Come, let’s go down; confuse each tongue, / So none can understand the words of anyone.”
Yahweh confused all earth’s speech; Babel got its name / They stopped the city-building, scattered o’er earth’s face
Shem’s line: Arpachshad, Shelah, Eber, Peleg came / Then Reu, Serug, Nahor continued after them
Nahor fathered Terah, who had sons, all three / Abram, Nahor, Haran—his sons in the family tree
Haran fathered Lot; in Ur of Chaldees, his life was done / Terah, his father, lived on, though Haran was gone
Abram wed Sarai; she bore no child, was barren / Nahor wed Milcah, the daughter of Haran
Terah took Abram, Lot, Sarai from Ur, bound for Canaan / They reached Haran, settled there, and made it their abode
Terah’s lifespan totaled two hundred five years / Terah spent his years in Haran, then died there
Yahweh said, “Leave country, kin, your father’s house; go where I will show” / Great nation, name great; blessers blessed, scorners cursed; all earth blessed through you
Abram went as told by Yahweh; Lot, Sarai by his side / With goods and all their people, into Canaan they arrived
Yahweh appeared: “This land I’ll give your offspring,” Yahweh declared / Abram then built an altar to Yahweh, who had appeared
East of Bethel, he pitched his tent on the ground / He built an altar, called Yahweh’s name, then southward bound
Severe famine sent him down to Egypt, a foreigner to live / Say you're my sister; they’ll kill me, spare you; let me live
Pharaoh’s princes praised her; she was taken to his home / For her sake, Pharaoh dealt well; Abram had flocks, servants of his own
Yahweh afflicted Pharaoh’s house with great plagues severe / Because of Sarai, Abram’s wife, who was taken there
Pharaoh asked, “Why didn’t you tell me she’s your wife? Why say so?” / “Why say ‘she’s my sister,’ so I took her as wife? Take her; go”
Pharaoh ordered men to escort them from Egypt’s land / They led Abram, Sarai, and all his goods in hand
From Egypt Abram went up with his wife and Lot in tow / All that he had came with him as southward they did go
He returned from South to Bethel, where his tent had been before / At altar between Bethel and Ai, called Yahweh’s name once more
Their herds and goods were vast; the land could not contain / Their herdsmen quarreled; together they could not remain
No strife between us or herdsmen; we’re kin, let it not grow / If you go left, I go right; if right, left I will go
Lot chose the well-watered Jordan plain; eastward he went away / His tent reached Sodom; its men sinned against Yahweh
Yahweh promised Abram all the land within his sight / To him and to his offspring as a lasting right
Your offspring like the earth’s dust, too vast for men to count / “Walk through its length and width; I give it,” Yahweh announced
Abram moved his tent to Mamre, in Hebron’s ground / There built an altar to Yahweh, where he settled down
Four kings made war on five, who served Chedorlaomer twelve years / In year thirteen, the five rebelled; their service ended there
Chedorlaomer and his kings set out to campaign / They struck the peoples through the hills and desert plain
The five kings faced the four in Siddim’s battlefield / They arrayed against them there, four kings against five in the field
Sodom and Gomorrah’s kings fled from battle, some fell down / In Siddim’s tar pits; others fled to hills around
They took Sodom and Gomorrah’s food and goods, left stores bare / They captured Lot and all his goods, caught in the raiders’ snare
An escapee told Abram Lot was seized and dragged away / He led three hundred eighteen trained men and gave chase that day
He split his force and struck them beneath the cover of night / Then he chased them to Hobah, and all the kings took flight
Abram brought Lot, goods, women, all the people back / His allies Mamre, Eshcol, Aner backed him
Melchizedek brought bread and wine, priest of God Most High / He blessed Abram and God, who gave foes; Abram gave a tithe
The king of Sodom met Abram, his proposal made / “Give me the people; take the goods for yourself,” he said
By Yahweh, I take nothing, lest you claim I grew rich from you / Except young men’s eaten food; my allies’ shares are due
Fear not, Abram; I’m your shield, your exceedingly great reward. / “Childless, Lord Yahweh, what give? Eliezer, my heir,” I implored.
Yahweh told Abram, “Your own body will bring forth your heir.” / Then Yahweh led him out beneath the open air.
“Count the stars, if you are able; your offspring will match their size.” / Abram believed; Yahweh counted him righteous in His eyes.
“I am Yahweh; from Ur I brought you this land to own.” / Abram then asked, “Lord Yahweh, how will I know?”
He split the beasts in two, each half set opposite on the ground. / He left the birds whole, drove prey away as they swooped down.
Offspring live as foreigners, serve them, four hundred years oppressed. / I'll judge the nation they serve; they'll leave with great wealth amassed.
Yahweh said, “You’ll go to your fathers in peace.” / “In old age, you’ll be buried; your days will cease.”
Your offspring return in generation four. / When Amorite iniquity is full, not before.
Furnace smoked; a torch aflame passed between pieces that night. / Yahweh made a covenant, gave Abram’s offspring land outright.
Childless Sarai gave Hagar, her Egyptian maid, as wife / Abram went in to her; she conceived, carrying life
Sarai said, “This wrong is yours; may Yahweh judge between us” / He said, “Do what seems good”; she dealt harshly, and Hagar fled from her
Yahweh’s angel found her, asked where she came from, where she’d fly / She answered, “I flee now from my mistress Sarai”
“Return to your mistress; submit beneath her hands” / Beer Lahai Roi lay between Kadesh and Bered’s lands
He promised Hagar offspring would multiply and grow / Beyond all counting’s reach, too many to ever know
“Call him Ishmael; Yahweh has heard your pain,” the angel spoke / His hand against all men; men’s hands against him; brothers all opposed
Hagar called Yahweh, “You are a God who sees,” who spoke to her / She asked, “Have I even stayed alive after seeing him there?”
Hagar bore Abram a son, as the angel foretold / Abram named the boy Ishmael, as Hagar had been told
At ninety-nine, Yahweh to Abram appeared / “I am God Almighty; walk before me, blameless,” declared
God pledged his covenant; Abram’s seed would vastly abound / And Abram then fell on his face, bowing low to the ground
God called him Abraham; many nations would descend his line / He’d be exceedingly fruitful; kings from him would come in time
His offspring through their generations: covenant secure / He’d be their God; Canaan theirs, possession to endure
Each male must be circumcised, the covenant’s command / The uncircumcised male would be cut off from his band
God named Sarai Sarah, blessed her; Abraham’s son she’d bear / Mother of nations, kings of all peoples would come from her
He fell on his face, then laughed: “Can a hundred-year-old conceive?” / “Could Sarah at ninety give birth?” he asked, “Could that be?”
Sarah would bear Abraham a son; Isaac would be his name / God’s everlasting covenant with Isaac’s seed would remain
God heard Abraham on Ishmael; he’d bless him, make him thrive / Twelve princes and a great nation from him would arise
Sarah would bear Isaac next year, as God said she’d do / Then God went up from Abraham when his speech was through
Abraham circumcised himself and Ishmael, as God planned / That day, all house-born and bought were circumcised by his hand
Yahweh appeared to him at Mamre’s oaks; three men stood near / He ran out to meet them, then bowed low as they appeared
He asked them to stay, offered water, rest, and bread / They agreed: “Very well; do just as you have said”
Sarah kneaded fine meal; Abraham prepared the feast / He served milk, butter, calf; beneath the tree they feasted
They asked where Sarah was; Abraham said, “She’s there” / Yahweh said, “I’ll return next year; a son she’ll bear”
Sarah heard and laughed within, her doubt concealed / Both were old; Sarah’s womb could no child now yield
Yahweh asked, “Why did she laugh? Is anything too hard for me?” / At the set time I’ll return; Sarah will bear a son, you’ll see
Sarah, afraid, said, “I didn’t laugh,” and denied / Yahweh said, “No, but you did laugh,” and replied
The men rose, looked toward Sodom, then set out from that place / Abraham walked with them to see them on their way
“Will I hide what I do? Great, mighty nation shall rise” / “All nations blessed through him; his house keeps Yahweh’s way, does right”
The outcry from Sodom and Gomorrah was great / Their grievous sin: he’d go see if reports held weight
Abraham asked, “Will you destroy the righteous there / Along with the wicked? Judge of all earth, act fair.”
Yahweh said, “If fifty righteous are found in the town / I’ll spare the whole place for their sake, not cast it down”
Abraham asked of forty-five, then forty alone / Yahweh would spare the city for each number shown
He asked thirty, twenty, then ten—the descending score / Yahweh would not destroy for each count, as before
Yahweh departed when their speaking was through / Abraham returned to his place, as he would do
Two angels came at evening; Lot welcomed them to stay / He baked unleavened bread and served them; they ate
Before they slept, Sodom’s men encircled Lot’s front door / “Bring out your guests; we want to lie with them,” they roared
He begged, “Do no wicked thing”; his two virgin daughters, too / He offered in their place, but would not yield his guests to you
They pressed hard at the door; the angels pulled Lot inside / They shut it, struck them blind—small, great, all who stood outside
The angels said, “Bring all your kin; the outcry’s grown too great” / “Yahweh sent us to destroy this place”—the city’s fate
Lot warned his sons-in-law: “Yahweh will destroy this town” / They thought his words were joking; they heard no warning sound
At dawn the angels hurried Lot; he lingered in delay / Yahweh showed mercy, took their hands, and led them all away
The angels said, “Flee to the mountains; don’t look behind” / He asked for Zoar; they spared it till he arrived
When Lot reached Zoar, Yahweh rained sulfur and fire down / Sodom, Gomorrah, plain, people and crops were overthrown
Lot’s wife looked back as they fled from the burning site / She became a pillar of salt, fixed upright
Abraham saw the smoke rise like a furnace in the sky / God remembered Abraham and brought Lot out alive
Afraid to stay in Zoar, Lot climbed the mountain high / He and his daughters lived in a cave nearby
The firstborn made him drink wine, then lay with him there / He knew not when she lay or rose, unaware
And the next night they made Lot drink wine once again / The younger lay with him; he knew not when she'd rise again
Lot’s daughters conceived by their father in the cave / Each of them carried his child, the offspring he gave
The firstborn bore Moab, father of the Moabites / The younger bore Ben Ammi, father of Ammonites
Abraham lived as a foreigner in Gerar / He called Sarah his sister; the king took her from there
God warned him in a dream that he would lose his life / For taking the woman who was another man’s wife
He claimed an innocent heart; God kept him from sin / “Restore her, or death will come for you and those within.”
Abimelech told his servants what God had decreed / Then charged Abraham, “You brought guilt on my realm and me.”
“I feared they’d kill me for Sarah,” Abraham made clear / “I asked my half-sister, ‘Say he’s my brother far and near.’”
He restored Sarah and gave sheep, cattle, servants too / “My land is before you; you may dwell where you choose.”
I gave your brother a thousand silver pieces outright / Before all who are with you, you’re vindicated in their sight
Abraham prayed; God healed the king and his spouse / His wife and female servants bore children in his house.
Yahweh kept His promise at the time He’d set / Sarah bore old Abraham a son, as He had said
Abraham called his son Isaac, as the record states / On day eight he circumcised him, as God’s command dictates
“God made me laugh,” Sarah said; all who hear will laugh with me / “Who’d tell Abraham Sarah would nurse children? Now you see”
When Isaac grew and was weaned, Abraham marked the day / He held a great feast for his son, as Isaac was weaned that day
Hagar the Egyptian bore Abraham a son / Sarah saw the boy of Hagar mock, the one
She said, “Cast out this servant and her son from here” / “Her son won’t be heir with Isaac, my son and heir”
God said, “Don’t grieve for the boy or servant; listen to her voice” / “Your offspring will be named through Isaac—that is my choice”
God promised the servant’s son would become a nation / Because he was Abraham’s child—the stated reason
Abraham sent them bread and the water as they left home / Water ran dry; she left him beneath a shrub, sat far, wept alone
God’s angel called Hagar: “Don’t fear; the boy’s voice God heard” / “Lift up the boy; I’ll make him a great nation,” God’s word
God opened Hagar’s eyes; she saw a well right there / She filled the container, gave the boy a drink with care
God was with him; he grew an archer in the wild / His mother got an Egyptian wife for her child
Abimelech and Phicol said, “God is with you in all you do” / “Swear no false dealings with us, our sons, their sons; return kindness too”
Abraham said, “Your servants seized my well and took it away” / Abimelech said, “I didn’t know; I heard of it today”
At Beersheba Abraham planted a tamarisk tree / And called on Yahweh, the Everlasting God, there
God puts Abraham to the test, then lays on him this demand / “Take Isaac, only son you love, as burnt offering in the land”
He rose early with Isaac, two young men in tow / He split the wood and went where God told him to go
On day three he saw the place far off; it came into view / “Stay with the donkey; the boy and I will worship, return to you”
Isaac carried wood, asked, “Where’s the lamb? We have none.” / Abraham answered, “God will provide the lamb, my son.”
At God’s chosen place, he built the altar, bound Isaac tight / He laid him on the wood and took the knife to end his life
Yahweh’s angel called, “Do not harm the boy; let him be” / “I know you fear God; you did not withhold your only son from me”
Abraham saw behind him a ram, its horns caught fast / He went and took it from the thicket’s tangled grasp
He offered up the ram as burnt offering instead / Isaac was spared, as Yahweh’s angel had said
He gave that place the name “Yahweh Will Provide” / “On Yahweh’s mountain, the need will be supplied”
God swore, “I’ll multiply all your offspring like stars and sand” / “Foes’ gates theirs; all nations blessed through them, since you obeyed command”
He returned to the young men; they rose and went that day / Together they went to Beersheba, where Abraham would stay
Sarah lived one hundred twenty-seven years of age / She died in Canaan, Hebron—Kiriath Arba’s place
Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, his wife / He wept for her, grieving the loss of her life
He told the Hittites, “I’m a foreigner among you” / “Give me a place to bury my dead out of view”
They called him prince of God, and offered their best / “None would withhold a tomb; bury your dead,” they professed
He asked them, “Let Ephron sell the cave to me” / “At Machpelah’s field-end, full price was my plea”
Ephron publicly offered Abraham the field / The cave within it, too, he offered to yield
Four hundred shekels of silver, that was the full price / Abraham weighed it; the field and cave were now his outright
Abraham buried Sarah where Machpelah’s cave lay / At Mamre, which is Hebron, in Canaan that day
Old Abraham, blessed by Yahweh, gave his chief servant command / Seek Isaac a wife among his kin, not Canaan’s daughters’ hand
The servant asked, “If she won’t follow, what should I do? / Must I bring Isaac back to the land you once knew?”
“Don’t bring my son back to the land that was my home / He swore this land to my offspring as their own”
Yahweh will send His angel ahead to take the lead / If she refuses, from your oath you will be freed
He swore, took ten camels and gifts, set out on the road / To Nahor’s city, bearing his master’s load
At the well he prayed to Yahweh, Abraham’s God, “Hear my plea / Let her be Isaac’s chosen wife if she waters them and me”
At the spring, before his prayer was finished, Rebekah drew near / Bethuel’s daughter, Nahor’s granddaughter—Abraham’s kin stood there
He asked her for a drink; she let the water flow to him / Then offered to draw for his camels, supplying them
She drew for all his camels till each had drunk its fill / He watched in silence, wondered if Yahweh made it well
He gave her ring and bracelets, asked whose daughter she might be / And if her father’s house had enough room for us to stay
She said, “Bethuel’s daughter; we have lodging, straw, and feed / And room enough to lodge,” she said, answering his need
He bowed and blessed Yahweh, for His kindness remained / His truth toward Abraham, his master, was sustained
Rebekah told her family what had occurred / Laban welcomed the servant and his men when he heard
He would not eat before his message had been shared / “I am Abraham’s servant,” he declared
He said Yahweh had blessed his master, made him great / And gave all he owned to Isaac, his heir to the estate
He told his prayer, her offer, and her family tree / “Will you deal kindly and truly with my master? Answer, please.”
Laban and Bethuel both said, “Yahweh has shown the way” / “Take Rebekah as Isaac’s wife”; he bowed, praised Yahweh
He gave Rebekah and her kin gifts, then they took rest / At morning he asked, “Send me to my master”—his request
Her kin asked her to stay a few days—ten at least, they say / “Yahweh has prospered my way, so send me away”
They asked if she would go; she answered, “I will go” / They blessed her: tens of thousands; her offspring would master foes
Isaac saw the camels coming in the fading light / “Who is that man?” “My master”; she veiled herself from sight
The servant told Isaac all he’d done; he took her as his bride / He loved and wed Rebekah; comfort came when his mother died
While still alive, he placed all he had in Isaac’s hand / His concubines’ sons got gifts, sent east from that land
Isaac and Ishmael buried Abraham in the cave / At Machpelah, with Sarah, his wife, sharing that grave
Abraham died; God blessed Isaac, his son / At Beer Lahai Roi, there Isaac lived on
Twelve princes from Ishmael are listed by their nations / His years: one hundred thirty-seven; he died, joined his relations
At forty, Isaac took Rebekah as his wife / Bethuel’s daughter, Laban’s sister, joined his life
Rebekah was barren; Isaac prayed and pleaded / Yahweh was entreated, and Rebekah conceived
The children struggled within; she asked Yahweh why / “If it is like this, why do I live?” was her cry
Two nations and two peoples were growing, one stronger / The elder would then serve the younger of them
Esau came out red, like a hairy garment worn / Jacob came gripping Esau’s heel when he was born
Esau hunted the field; Isaac loved him for game / Jacob lived quiet in tents; Rebekah loved him the same
Jacob boiled stew; Esau came in from the field / “Please feed me some red stew; I’m famished,” he appealed
Jacob told Esau, “Sell your birthright first to me” / Esau said, “I’m about to die; what good can it be?”
Jacob said, “Swear it to me first”; Esau swore / He sold his birthright—the thing Jacob asked for
Jacob gave him bread and lentil stew to eat / Esau ate and drank, then left, his birthright held cheap
Famine struck; to Gerar Isaac made his way / To Abimelech, Philistine king, he came to stay
Yahweh said, “Don’t go to Egypt; live here; I’ll stay with you” / “I’ll bless you, grant lands; Abraham’s oath, seed, stars; all nations too”
When asked, Isaac called Rebekah sister, a lie / He feared they’d kill him; dared not say she was his wife
Abimelech saw Isaac caress Rebekah, asked why / Isaac admitted fear; the king said, “You’d bring guilt; touch them, die”
Isaac sowed and reaped a hundredfold across the land / Yahweh blessed him; he grew great; Philistines envied him
Philistines stopped Abraham’s wells, filled them with clay / Abimelech said, “You’re mightier than we; go away”
He camped in Gerar’s valley; dug his father’s wells below / His men found water; herdsmen disputed Esek and Sitnah’s flow
He dug a well none disputed; Rehoboth was its name / “Yahweh made room; we’ll bear fruit here,” Isaac then proclaimed
At Beersheba, Yahweh said, “Your father’s God I am” / “Fear not; I’m with you; bless, multiply your seed for Abraham”
He built an altar, called on Yahweh’s name there / He pitched his tent; his servants dug a well nearby
Abimelech came from Gerar with his companions near / Isaac asked, “You hate me, sent me away; why are you here?”
They said, “We saw Yahweh with you; swear no harm, make covenant sure” / “We touched you not, did only good; Yahweh’s blessing is yours”
Isaac made a feast; they ate and drank at ease / At dawn they swore an oath, then all left in peace
That day his servants found water; he named it Shibah / The city then took its name from it: Beersheba
Forty, Esau wed Hittite wives, Judith, Basemath by name / Judith and Basemath grieved Isaac and Rebekah the same
Old, dim-eyed Isaac called Esau, his elder son, near; / “I don’t know the day I’ll die; its date is unclear.”
“Go hunt and bring me game; prepare the meal I prize. / Then I may bless you ere death closes my eyes.”
Rebekah heard Isaac tell Esau what he desired; / She told young Jacob what his father required.
“Bring two young goats; I’ll cook what your father loves, my son; / Then take it in, so Isaac’s blessing can be won.”
“If touched, I’ll seem a cheat, bring a curse, not blessing,” he feared; / “Let your curse fall on me; obey, go fetch,” his mother urged.
Jacob brought the goats; she cooked, dressed him in Esau’s clothes. / She covered hands and neck with goat skins, so touch would not expose.
He came to Isaac, claiming, “I’m Esau, your eldest one.” / He asked him, “Eat this food, then bless me when you’re done.”
“How did you find it so quickly?” Isaac inquired. / “Yahweh your God gave me success,” Jacob replied.
Isaac said, “The voice is Jacob’s; Esau’s hands I feel.” / He asked, “Are you Esau?” “I am,” Jacob lied, truth concealed.
Isaac ate and drank, then asked his son to kiss his face; / He smelled Esau’s clothes and blessed him with grace.
“May God give dew, earth’s fatness, grain and wine across your land; / Nations bow; kin serve; cursers cursed, blessers blessed by God’s hand.”
Esau returned from hunting with venison to eat; / “Eat, father, then bless me,” he asked, bringing the meat.
“Who are you?” “I am Esau, your firstborn,” was his reply; / Isaac trembled: “He who took the blessing stays blessed,” he cried.
Esau cried, “Oh, bless me too!” in such bitter pain; / “Your brother, by deceit, took your blessing,” Isaac explained.
“Twice Jacob supplanted me; my birthright and blessing he seized. / Have you kept a blessing for me?” Esau then asked, displeased.
“I made him lord of you, with grain and wine in store; / What then can I do for you, my son—what more?”
Esau begged for blessing, weeping as he spoke; / “You’ll live by sword, serve him, then shake his yoke,” Isaac said.
Esau hated Jacob for the blessing he received; / He planned to kill him once his father’s mourning ceased.
Rebekah warned Jacob, “Flee to Laban in Haran; stay; / Until your brother’s anger has at last turned away.”
“I’ll send for you when his anger is relieved; / Why should I be of both sons in one day bereaved?”
Rebekah told Isaac, “Heth’s daughters weary me; / If Jacob weds one, what good will my life be?”
Isaac sent Jacob to Paddan; Canaanite wives he barred / “Take Laban’s daughters for your wife,” Isaac then declared
May God make you fruitful, multiply, a host of peoples rise / Abraham’s blessing, land God gave to you and yours, your prize
Esau saw Jacob obey his father and his mother / Then took Mahalath, Ishmael’s daughter, one more wife among others
Jacob went toward Haran, stopped as the daylight died / He set a stone beneath his head, and slept through the night
He dreamed a stairway rose from earth to heaven’s height / God’s angels climbed and then descended in his sight
“I am Yahweh, God of Abraham, your father, and Isaac too” / “I’ll give land to you and seed; all families blessed in both through you.”
“I’ll keep you wherever you go, bring you back once more” / “I won’t leave till I’ve done what I spoke before”
He woke, afraid: “Yahweh’s here; I didn’t know—God’s house, heaven’s gate!” / He raised the stone as pillar, poured oil; named that place Bethel
If God stays, guards my way, feeds, clothes, and brings me home safe, I swear / Then Yahweh will be my God; this pillar, God’s house; a tenth I’ll share
Jacob reached the eastern land, where three flocks gathered round / A massive stone lay on the well’s mouth, there on the ground
“We’re from Haran; we know Laban,” the shepherds made clear / “He’s well; his daughter Rachel comes with sheep, drawing near”
Jacob urged, “It’s midday; water sheep, then go and feed” / They said, “We wait till all flocks gather; then water as they need”
Rachel came with father’s sheep; Jacob rolled the stone / He watered Laban’s flock, the sheep that Laban owned
Jacob kissed Rachel, raised his voice, and wept as well / He said, “I’m kin, Rebekah’s son”; she ran, her father to tell
Laban brought him to his house, heard all Jacob had to tell / Called him bone and flesh; a month with him he dwelled
Laban asked; Jacob pledged seven years for Rachel’s hand / For Rachel, his younger daughter, Laban agreed to the demand
Jacob served seven years for Rachel, loving her from the start / They seemed but a few days to him, for love filled up his heart
Jacob asked for his wife; Laban held a feast for the bride / At evening he brought Leah; Zilpah served her at her side
At dawn Jacob found Leah, and asked why he was misled / “I served with you for Rachel; why deceive me?” Jacob said
Laban said, “Here, firstborn before younger is the way we go” / “Fulfill her week; then Rachel’s yours; seven more years you owe”
He fulfilled her week; Laban gave Rachel to him as wife / Bilhah served Rachel; he loved her more, served seven more years of life
Yahweh saw Leah hated; womb opened; Rachel barren remained / Named Reuben: Yahweh saw affliction; husband loves me, she explained
She named him Simeon: Yahweh heard she was hated, gave another son to me / The third she named Levi: “Three sons; now my husband will be joined to me”
She bore Judah, saying, “This time Yahweh I will praise” / Then Leah stopped from bearing, ending her childbearing days
Rachel envied her sister, childless, bereft / “Give me children, Jacob, or death is what’s left.”
Jacob’s anger burned: “Am I in God’s place, who withheld / The fruit of the womb from you?” His reply came out held.
Rachel gave Bilhah, her maid, to Jacob to wed, / That she might bear children on Rachel’s knees instead.
Bilhah bore Dan; Rachel said, “God judged me” / “He then heard my voice and gave a son to me.”
Bilhah bore Naphtali; Rachel spoke of the fight / “I wrestled with my sister and prevailed”—that night.
Leah ceased bearing; her servant Zilpah she chose / And gave her to Jacob as wife, so offspring arose.
Zilpah bore Gad; “How fortunate!” Leah proclaimed / Asher came; “The daughters call me happy,” she claimed.
Reuben brought mandrakes to Leah from the field / Rachel asked Leah, “Some of those, would you yield?”
Leah said, “You took my husband; my son’s mandrakes too?” / Rachel said, “For your son’s mandrakes, tonight he’ll come to you.”
“Issachar she named; God gave my hire, maid to husband I gave” / “Zebulun, Dinah she named; six sons, with me he stayed.”
God remembered Rachel, heard her; new life had begun / She bore Joseph; “My reproach is gone; Yahweh, add one more son.”
After Joseph’s birth, Jacob asked Laban to release / His wives and children; let me go to my own country, please.
Laban asked Jacob to stay; by divining, he’d known / Yahweh blessed him; his flocks and his wealth had grown.
“You know how all your flocks fared with me; from few they grew” / “Yahweh blessed wherever I turned; when provide for my own house too?”
“Marked goats and black sheep are my hire,” Jacob declared / “Unmarked with me is theft; my right answers; Laban agreed.”
Laban removed marked goats, black sheep, and gave them to his sons / Three days’ journey between them; Jacob fed the flock that remained.
Jacob peeled poplar, almond, plane rods, white streaks in view / At troughs the flocks conceived; streaked, speckled, spotted young grew.
Weak stock went to Laban; the strong became Jacob’s own / His flocks, servants, camels, donkeys increased and had grown.
His sons said Jacob took their father’s wealth as prize / Laban’s face no longer held the old regard in his eyes
Yahweh said, “Return to your fathers’ land again / Go back among your relatives; I’ll be with you then”
“God stayed with me, though your father cheated me all along / He changed my wages ten times; God kept me safe and strong”
“God guarded me and gave the flocks, as you both can see / In dreams the angel showed the goats, streaked, speckled too”
“I am Bethel’s God; I saw what Laban put you through / Return now to your birthplace; go, as I command you”
“No share; he treats us like strangers, used our money, sold / God’s wealth is ours and our children’s; do as you’ve been told”
He crossed the River, fled with all, toward Gilead’s height / Rachel stole father’s gods while Laban sheared, out of sight
Laban heard on the third day; seven days he gave chase / He caught Jacob in Gilead’s mountains, face to face
God warned Laban in a dream: “Take care what you may say— / Speak neither good nor bad to Jacob on your way”
“You tricked me and stole my gods,” Laban cried aloud / “God warned me: speak no good or bad,” he avowed
“I fled, afraid you’d take your daughters by force through my doors / Whoever has your gods shall die; search all our stores”
He searched the tents; Rachel sat on gods in camel gear / “I cannot rise; my period’s here,” she said; he found none there
“Show what household goods you found,” Jacob demanded now / Laban had nothing to display or set before the crowd
“Twenty years: day drought, night frost; my sleep fled my sight / Fourteen for daughters, six for flocks; I served you outright”
“The God of Abraham, Isaac’s Fear, came to my aid / He saw my toil and affliction, your deeds he decried”
“Your daughters, children, flocks, all that you see are mine / Now come, let’s make a covenant, witness between us two”
Jacob set a stone upright, a pillar on the ground / His kin and Laban piled stones; a heap stood all around
“This heap stands witness between us,” Laban said, “as we part / May Yahweh watch between us when we’re far apart”
“If you afflict my daughters or take other wives / No man is with us; God witnesses what transpires”
“No crossing for harm,” Laban said, the boundary clear / “God judge between us,” he said; Jacob swore by Isaac’s Fear
Jacob offered sacrifice; his kin ate bread / They stayed all night upon the mountain where they’d fed
At dawn Laban kissed his sons and daughters, blessed them there / Then left and headed back to his own familiar place
God’s angels met with Jacob; “God’s army,” he declared / He named that place Mahanaim; its name he did declare
He sent to Esau: “With Laban I have stayed” / “I have flocks and servants; your favor I seek, I pray”
The messengers returned: “Esau is drawing near” / “Four hundred men are with him, and they are coming here”
Afraid, he split his folk and flocks in two camps either side / If Esau strikes one company, the other may survive
God of Abraham and Isaac called me back; promised aid / I’m unworthy of Your kindness; keep Esau’s hand at bay
He sent his herds ahead as gifts, spaced out along the route / “Your servant Jacob follows, my lord,” the servants called out
He took his wives, sons, servants, all he had to Jabbok’s ford / He sent them over; Jacob stood alone upon the shore
Jacob wrestled with a man until the break of light / The man saw he could not prevail against him in the fight
He touched Jacob’s thigh; it strained: “The day breaks; let me go” / Jacob said, “I won’t let you go unless you bless me so”
He asked, “What is your name?” “Jacob,” his answer came / He named him Israel: “With God and men you fought, overcame”
Jacob asked, “Please tell your name.” “Why ask?” came the reply / He blessed him there; his name he did not supply
He named that place Peniel: “I saw God face to face” / “My life was preserved,” he said; he came away safe
At sunrise Jacob passed Peniel, limping on his way / Israel’s children don’t eat hip sinew where he touched his thigh
Jacob saw Esau approach with four hundred men / He split the children among Leah, Rachel, servants then
Jacob went ahead, bowed seven times to the ground / Till he came near to his brother, head bowed down
Esau ran, embraced him, kissed him, held him near / They wept together, both, their faces wet with tears
Esau asked who the women and children were he saw / Jacob said, “God gave these children graciously”; servants bowed low
Esau asked what the company was for, and why / Jacob said, “To find favor in my lord’s eye”
Esau said, “I have enough, my brother; let your things stay with thee” / Jacob urged, “Please take my gift; God's face I saw in yours; you pleased me”
Esau said, “Let’s take our journey, and I’ll go before you” / Jacob said, “If driven hard one day, the young flocks all die too”
Esau offered men; Jacob declined; Esau turned toward Seir / Jacob reached Succoth, built a house and shelters there
Jacob came into Shechem, and bought a land plot / He raised an altar, called El Elohe Israel on that spot
Dinah went out to see the daughters living there / Shechem took her, lay with her, and humbled her
Shechem loved her, asked his father to let them wed / “Get me this young lady as a wife,” he had then said
Jacob heard Shechem had defiled Dinah, lips sealed / Till his sons returned from their livestock in the field
Hamor, Shechem’s father, came to Jacob to speak / Dinah’s brothers grieved, enraged; their anger ran deep
Hamor asked, “Give Dinah to Shechem as his bride” / “Wed our families; live and trade here side by side”
Shechem asked their favor, sought Dinah as his choice / “Ask me a great dowry; I will pay its price”
“Circumcise every male, and one people we will be” / “If not, we’ll take our sister, then from your city flee”
Hamor and Shechem agreed that they would proceed / Shechem did not delay; he acted with speed
They said, “Be circumcised; our peoples will be one” / To townsmen: “Their livestock and goods will be our own”
The city’s men listened to Hamor and Shechem’s plea / Every male was circumcised, as they agreed
On the third day, while sore, the town was caught unaware / They killed each male, Hamor, Shechem, took Dinah from there
They seized the flocks, herds, donkeys, wealth from field and town / Took wives and children captive, stripped each house down
“You’ve made me odious; I’m few; they’ll strike my house” / They asked, “Should he deal with our sister as a prostitute?”
God said, “Go to Bethel, live there, and make your abode; / Build an altar to God who met you fleeing Esau on the road.”
“Put foreign gods away; purify, change garments, I say; / Let’s rise to Bethel; God answered me distressed, stayed by me on way.”
All foreign gods and rings from ears they placed in Jacob’s hand; / He hid them ’neath the oak beside Shechem in the land.
They journeyed on; God’s terror struck the cities far and near; / No town pursued the sons of Jacob, held back by fear.
Jacob built an altar there; El Beth El he named the site; / God had revealed himself there when he fled his brother’s sight.
Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, died; beneath Bethel’s oak / They buried her; Allon Bacuth was the name they spoke.
From Paddan Aram God appeared and blessed him again; / “You’ll no longer be called Jacob; Israel is your name.”
“I am God Almighty; bear fruit; nations and kings spring from thee; / The land of Abraham and Isaac goes to you and to your seed.”
After God went up, Jacob raised a pillar made of stone; / He poured oil and a drink offering, made Bethel’s name known.
On the way to Ephrath, Rachel labored hard in pain; / The midwife said, “Do not fear; you shall bear a son again.”
She named the child Benoni as she breathed her last that day; / Jacob named him Benjamin, set a pillar where she lay.
Reuben lay with Bilhah, his father’s concubine there; / Israel heard; Jacob’s sons were twelve, the text declares.
Jacob came to Isaac, who lived a hundred eighty years; / Esau and Jacob buried him, and he joined his peers.
Esau wed Adah, Basemath, Oholibamah as brides / From the Hittite, the Hivite, and the Ishmaelite tribes
Adah bore Eliphaz; and Reuel from Basemath was born / In Canaan, Oholibamah bore Jeush, Jalam, Korah in turn
Esau took his household, flocks, and goods away / He left his brother Jacob, going his separate way
Their substance grew too great to share one dwelling place / The land could not bear their livestock or give them space
Esau lived in Seir’s hills, his mountain home / Esau is Edom, by that name he was known
Eliphaz’s sons: Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, Kenaz / Timna bore Amalek, the son of Eliphaz
Reuel's sons: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, Mizzah, all four / Basemath bore them; her name is kept in the record
Esau’s descendants were chiefs throughout Edom’s ground / Listed by family, each name was written down
Seir’s Horite clans were fully traced through their kin / Seven chief families were listed within
Anah found hot springs while tending donkeys there / His father Zibeon owned them, entrusted to his care
Edom's kings ruled before Israel's kingly reign / The chapter names each ruler, listing each by name
Bela, son of Beor, ruled Edom and wore the crown / Dinhabah was the city, its name written down
Bela died; Jobab then took the throne instead / Zerah's son from Bozrah became Edom's next head
Then Jobab died, and Husham came to take the crown / From Temanites’ land, he ruled Edom’s ground
Hadad, Bedad’s son, then ruled from Avith town / He struck Midian in Moab’s field, as records write it down
Hadad died; Samlah followed, taking the reign / From Masrekah, he governed Edom's domain
And when Samlah had died, Shaul then came to reign / Baal Hanan, Achbor’s son, next ruled Edom’s domain
When Baal Hanan died, Hadar ruled from Pau, his home / Edom’s chiefs were listed by the homes they’d known
At seventeen, Joseph fed the flock with brothers there / He brought his father their bad report, made clear
Israel loved Joseph more; a tunic of many hues / His brothers hated him; no peaceful words came through
He dreamed his sheaf stood; their sheaves bowed to his in the plain / They asked, “Will you reign and rule us?”—then hated him again
He dreamed sun, moon, eleven stars bowed to him overhead / His father scolded; brothers envied; the words stayed in his head
Israel sent him to see if flock and brothers were well / “Bring back word,” he said; Joseph set out to tell
A man directed Joseph to Dothan’s place / And he had found his brothers there, face to face
They planned to kill him, cast him in a pit below / And say a beast devoured him; see what his dreams would show
Reuben said, “Shed no blood; throw him in the pit instead” / He planned to bring him back to father, not leave him dead
They stripped his many-colored tunic from his back / And cast him in an empty pit, where water lacked
Judah urged them to sell Joseph as they sat down to their meal / He said, “He’s our brother, flesh of ours”; they agreed to the deal
Midianite merchants pulled Joseph out, sold him away / To Ishmaelites for twenty silver pieces they paid
Reuben came back, found Joseph gone, tore clothes in woe / “The child is no more; and I, where will I go?”
They killed a male goat; his tunic was blood-red / “We found this; examine: your son’s tunic or not?” they said
Jacob knew that a beast had torn Joseph apart / He mourned many days; would not let comfort reach his heart
In Egypt, Midianites sold Joseph to Pharaoh’s man / Potiphar, captain of the guard, was in command
Judah left his brothers, went to Hirah’s side / He took Shua’s daughter, and she became his wife
Judah’s wife bore three sons; Er came first in line / Onan came next, and Shelah followed in time
Judah gave Tamar to Er, his firstborn, as his wife / Er did evil in Yahweh’s sight and lost his life
Judah told Onan, “Raise offspring for your brother; do your part” / Onan knew that child would not be his, but his brother’s from the start
When he went in, Onan spilled his seed upon the ground / Yahweh killed him too; his evil brought him down
Judah sent her to her father’s house, a widow, to wait / When Shelah grew, he did not give him as her mate
After his wife died, Tamar heard Judah would shear / At Enaim she veiled on Timnah’s road and sat there
He thought she was a prostitute, her face veiled from view / Judah called, “Please come, let me come in to you”
Tamar wore her widow’s garments once again / Judah sent Hirah with the goat; he searched in vain
Hirah said, “No prostitute could be found anywhere” / Judah said, “Let her keep it, lest shame be ours to bear”
Three months later, Judah heard she was pregnant through prostitution / He ordered her brought out and burned: her execution
Tamar sent his signet, cord, and staff, and asked, “Whose could they be?” / “She’s more righteous than I; I kept Shelah from her,” Judah agreed
A hand emerged; they tied scarlet thread; it withdrew / Perez broke through; Zerah followed, thread-marked too
Joseph was brought down to Egypt; Potiphar bought him there / The Ishmaelites had brought him down, then sold him into his care
Potiphar made him overseer, put all his goods in his care / Yahweh blessed his house and field because Joseph was there
His master’s wife said, “Lie with me”; he would not comply / “He put all but you in my hand; how could I God defy?”
She spoke to Joseph every day; he would not comply / He went in to do his work; no men were there nearby
She caught him by his garment: “Lie with me!” she cried / He left it in her hand, then fled from her side
She told the men, “A Hebrew came to mock us, came to lie” / “I cried aloud; he left his garment, fled outside”
At home she told Potiphar, “He came to mock and lie” / “I cried aloud; he left his garment, then ran outside”
Potiphar grew angry and sent Joseph to a cell / The king’s own prisoners were bound there in that jail
The keeper favored Joseph, put prisoners in his charge / Yahweh made his work to prosper; his success grew large
Pharaoh grew angry; his chief officers were confined / The cupbearer and baker were locked up inside
The captain assigned both to Joseph’s care / He tended them through many prison days there
Both dreamed one night; at dawn, their grief showed clear / Joseph asked why sorrow clouded their cheer
They said, “We have dreamed; no one can interpret the dream.” / Joseph said, “Does God not interpret? Please tell me what you dreamed.”
Before him stood a vine with three branches, full in span / Budded, bloomed; ripe grapes pressed; the cup passed to his hand
Within three days, Pharaoh restores your place again / You’ll put his cup into his hand as you did then
Show kindness; tell Pharaoh; bring me out from there / I was stolen from the Hebrews; no wrong put me here
Three baskets of white bread were balanced on his head / Pharaoh’s baked food filled the top; birds ate it instead
Three baskets mean three days; your head he’ll take away / On a tree he’ll hang you; birds eat your flesh that day
At Pharaoh’s birthday feast, both heads were raised among his men / Cupbearer restored; baker hanged; he forgot Joseph then
After two full years, Pharaoh dreamed beside the stream / Seven sleek, fat cattle rose and fed in marshland green
Seven ugly, thin cattle followed, lean in size / They ate the sleek, fat seven before Pharaoh’s eyes
Seven good heads of grain grew on one stalk, healthy and full / The east-wind-blasted thin heads swallowed them all
At morning Pharaoh’s spirit troubled him, dismayed / No wise man or Egyptian mage could read what they conveyed
The cupbearer recalled Joseph interpreted their dreams / His and the baker’s in custody; both came true, it seems
Pharaoh summoned Joseph; they brought him from his cell / He shaved, changed clothes, then came before Pharaoh as well
Pharaoh recounted cattle, grain heads, east-wind-blown / No one could explain the dreams he had been shown
Joseph answered Pharaoh: “It isn’t in me;” / “God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace,” said he
Thin cattle and empty heads foretold famine ahead / They would follow seven good years, just as he said
God showed seven years of plenty throughout Egypt’s breadth / Then famine would consume the land with grievous dearth
The dream was doubled; by God the matter was ordained / He’d soon bring it to pass, as God had explained
Joseph advised, “Let a wise, discreet man oversee the state / Set the overseers throughout all the land, in every place”
“Take one fifth of Egypt’s produce in the good years of yield / Gather that share from every harvest in the field”

Weeping, “I am Joseph! Does my father still live?” / His brothers stood in terror, unable to reply
“Come near; I’m Joseph, your brother; here I stand / The very one you sold into Egypt’s land.”
Don’t grieve; God sent me ahead to preserve your lives / Through famine, by great deliverance, you’ll survive

Hurry, tell Father I rule; five famine years remain / Bring him and his household to Goshen; I’ll sustain
Your eyes and Benjamin’s see my mouth speaking clear / Hurry, tell Father my glory; bring him down here
He wept with Benjamin, held him in embrace / He kissed his brothers, and they talked face to face

They told Jacob Joseph lives and rules; he could not believe / When he saw the wagons Joseph sent, his spirit revived
“Enough—my son Joseph lives on,” Israel said / “I’ll go and see him before my days have fled.”
At Beersheba, Israel offered sacrifices to God / The God of Isaac, his father, is his God
God spoke to Israel in visions of the night / “Jacob, Jacob!” “Here I am,” he answered in the night
God said, “I am God, the God of your father,” spoke clear / “Don’t be afraid to go down to Egypt; do not fear”
“There I will make of you a great nation, too” / “I will go down into Egypt there with you”
God promised, “I will bring you up once more” / “And Joseph’s hand will close your eyes when life is o’er”
Jacob rose; his sons bore him, wives and children in tow / In Pharaoh’s wagons, sent to carry them below
They took their livestock and goods from Canaan’s land / With Jacob’s offspring, into Egypt came the band
Jacob sent Judah ahead to guide them through / They came to Goshen, as Judah was sent to do
Joseph went up to Goshen, to meet his father, chariot prepared / He met Israel his father and presented himself there
Joseph fell on Israel’s neck and wept a long while / All Jacob’s house came into Egypt: seventy in all
“Now let me die, since I have now seen your face;” / “You are still alive,” Israel said, there in that place

“When Pharaoh asks of your occupation, name your trade” / “‘We and our fathers kept livestock from youth till now,’ you say”
That lets you dwell there in Goshen, where you can remain / For shepherds are an abomination to Egyptians, it’s plain

“We’re shepherds; famine stripped Canaan’s pasturelands away” / “Let Goshen be our home; our flocks have nowhere left to graze”
“Let them all dwell in Goshen, Egypt’s best land there” / “Set able men to oversee my livestock with care”
Joseph brought his aged father Jacob to Pharaoh’s view / Jacob blessed: “One hundred thirty years; few, evil days I knew”
Joseph settled all his kin where richest fields were spread / He gave each household bread by size, and kept them fed
No bread in Egypt or Canaan; the famine laid them low / He gathered all grain-buying money; to Pharaoh’s house it flowed
Their money ran out; they brought their livestock in their need / Joseph traded bread for horses, flocks, herds, and donkeys indeed
“Our money’s spent; the herds are yours; just bodies, lands remain” / “Buy us and our land for bread and seed, that life and fields sustain”
He bought Egypt’s fields for Pharaoh; they became the king’s own / He moved them to cities; priests kept land, their portions from the throne
Joseph gave them seed to sow across each field / One fifth to Pharaoh, and four parts theirs to yield
“You saved our lives; we’ll serve Pharaoh,” the people agreed / The fifth became the law throughout the land by Joseph’s decree
Israel’s household settled in Goshen, goods in tow / They flourished, multiplied, and watched their numbers grow
Seventeen years in Egypt; one-forty-seven he attained / “Don’t bury me here; carry me where my fathers’ bones remain”

Jacob's sons rolled into Egypt's land, Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah hand in hand.
Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, all kin.

Pharaoh's decree, harsh and severe, “Every son, cast into the river, crystal clear.”
A man from Levi's clan took a Levi wife, She bore a son, hid him to save his life. Three months on, she could no longer hide, A basket with tar and pitch, she set him inside.

Yahweh's voice, "Speak what I say," Moses replied, "Pharaoh won't obey."

Moses and Aaron, they got a plan, Yahweh spoke, and they took their stand. "Moses, you're like God to Pharaoh's eyes, Aaron, your brother, will prophesy the skies.

Moses and Aaron, they did just that, Old but bold, no time for chat. Yahweh instructed, "When Pharaoh wants a show, Tell Aaron to cast his rod, let the serpent grow."
Into Pharaoh's court, Aaron threw it down, A rod to a serpent, right there in town. Pharaoh's magicians did the same trick, But Aaron's serpent swallowed theirs, quick.
Pharaoh's heart was stone, didn't heed the call, Yahweh said, "He's stubborn, won't budge at all. Meet him by the river, where he stands tall, Tell him Yahweh's command, the final call.
'Let my people go, to serve me in the wild,' Yet you haven't listened, Pharaoh, don't be beguiled. Strike the river with the rod in your hand, Turn waters to blood across this land.
Fish will perish, river foul and red, Egyptians will loathe to drink, they'll dread." Moses obeyed, Aaron stretched wide, Struck the waters, red tides won't hide.
Fish belly-up, river now foul, Egyptians thirsty, water makes them scowl. Magicians mimicked, but Pharaoh stayed hard, Turned away, didn't take it to heart.
Egyptians dug wells, searching for a sip, Seven days passed since Yahweh's mighty grip.
Yahweh spoke to Moses, "Head to Pharaoh's place, Tell him, 'Yahweh says, let my people embrace.' If he refuses, frogs will invade, They'll swarm his land, no place unscathed.

Aaron's hand stretched, frogs covered the land, The magicians matched with a similar stand. Pharaoh called out, "Plead with Yahweh for relief, Take these frogs away, end this grief."
Moses replied, "You choose the time, For frogs to leave, keep the rivers in line." Pharaoh said, "Tomorrow," Moses agreed, "So you know there's none like Yahweh indeed."
Frogs retreated, houses cleared, Gathered in heaps, the land was smeared. But Pharaoh's heart hardened, he wouldn't relent, As Yahweh foretold, his stubbornness spent.
"Tell Aaron," Yahweh said, "Dust to lice, Strike the earth, make Egypt pay the price." Aaron's rod struck, lice filled the air, Magicians failed, for this they couldn't prepare.
"This is God's finger," the magicians declared, But Pharaoh's heart hardened, he wasn't scared. "Go to Pharaoh," Yahweh called, "Let my people go, or flies will befall."
If you refuse, flies will swarm, But Goshen's land will remain warm. Separate my people, show my might, Tomorrow this sign, bring day from night."
Flies invaded Pharaoh's domain, Land corrupted, unbearable pain. "Go and sacrifice," Pharaoh said, "In this land, fulfill your dread."
Moses replied, "Not here, not right, Three days' journey, out of sight." Pharaoh allowed, but with a plea, "Pray for me, don't venture too free."

Yet Pharaoh's heart, once more turned cold, He wouldn't let them go, as the story's told.
