Gideon rose early, with his crew at the spring, Midian's camp up north, planning a swing. God said, "Too many with you, can't win like this, Or Israel might boast, their own strength they'll miss."
"Tell the fearful and trembling to retreat, Mount Gilead's their path, let them beat their feet." Twenty-two thousand turned back, ten thousand stayed, God spoke again, some would still be swayed.
"Take them to the water, I'll test them for you, Separate them out, see what they do." "Those who lap with their tongue, like a dog at play, Set them aside, they'll go your way."
Three hundred lapped, the rest knelt down, God said, "With these, you'll gain renown. Send the others home, keep just a few, Midian's yours with this loyal crew."
That night God whispered, "Go down to the camp, I've given it to you, don't let your faith damp." "If you're scared, take Purah, hear what they say, It'll strengthen your heart for the fray."
Gideon snuck with Purah, heard a dream unfold, A barley loaf rolled, struck a tent so bold. A fellow said, "That's Gideon's might, God's given Midian to him, they'll take flight."
Gideon worshiped, returned to his crowd, "Yahweh's granted us victory," he announced loud. He split them in three, trumpets in hand, Pitchers and torches, ready to stand.
"Watch me," said Gideon, "do as I do, When I blow my trumpet, you blow yours too." "Shout 'For Yahweh and Gideon!' make it ring, We'll surround the camp, fear we will bring."
They reached the camp at the middle watch, Broke pitchers, blew trumpets, the enemy they’d botch. "The sword of Yahweh and Gideon!" they cried, Midian trembled, their courage died.
Three hundred trumpets blew, chaos took hold, Yahweh turned swords on each other, the story told. Midian fled far, toward Zererah's land, Israel pursued with the upper hand.
Gideon called Ephraim, "Seize the waters wide, Chase Midian down, let none hide." Oreb and Zeeb, the princes they caught, At Oreb's rock and Zeeb's press, victory they brought.
Heads of the princes to Gideon they brought, Beyond the Jordan, God's victory wrought.

Ephraim's men questioned, "Why'd you leave us out the fight? When you battled Midian, you didn't call us, that ain't right." Gideon replied, "What have I done compared to your might? Your grapes' gleaning outshines my vineyard, that's my insight.
God gave you the Midian princes, Oreb and Zeeb in your hand, What could I do with a victory so grand?" Their anger cooled down, his words put them at ease, Gideon moved on, but he was not at peace.

He crossed the Jordan with three hundred men, tired but keen, "Give us bread," he asked Succoth, "for my men, who are lean. I'm chasing Zebah and Zalmunna, Midian's kings," But Succoth questioned, "Where's your proof of such things?"
Gideon warned, "When Yahweh hands them to me, I'll tear your flesh with thorns for your mockery." He went to Penuel, spoke the same lines, They answered with doubt, ignoring the signs.

He promised, "I'll return in peace and break your tower down," Zebah and Zalmunna camped with fifteen thousand, in Karkor town. Gideon struck their army, unprepared, unaware, Zebah and Zalmunna fled, but he caught them in his snare.

Returning from battle, he found Succoth's men, "See the kings you mocked me for, remember them?" He taught them a lesson with thorns, much pain, At Penuel, he broke the tower, their resistance was in vain.

To Zebah and Zalmunna, "Who were those you killed at Tabor?" "Men like you, royal in stature, nothing more." "They were my brothers," Gideon said with a tear, "If you'd spared their lives, you'd not face me here."

He called Jether, "Rise, make them pay the cost," But the boy hesitated, his courage almost lost. Zebah and Zalmunna taunted, "Man up, show your might," Gideon rose, took their lives, in the fading light.
Israel then asked Gideon to rule, "Be our king, You saved us from Midian, you did the right thing." Gideon declined, "Yahweh alone shall reign, But give me your earrings, from the battle's gain."
They spread a garment, gold poured like rain, Gideon made an ephod, which became a chain. Israel worshipped it, a snare in disguise, Forty years of peace, then Gideon's demise.
He had seventy sons, many wives to his name, His concubine bore Abimelech, adding to his fame. Gideon died, content, laid in his father's tomb, But Israel forgot, returning to idols too soon.
They turned to Baals, forgetting Yahweh's grace, Ignoring Gideon's deeds, they abandoned their place. No kindness to his house, though he was their guide, Israel drifted away, with Yahweh set aside.
Abimelech rolled to Shechem with a plan so sly, To his mother's kin, said, "Let me testify.
"Seventy rulers or just one from your own? I'm your flesh and bone, not just some clone."
His family sold the pitch, "He's our blood, our kin." Seventy silver coins got him reckless men.
At Ophrah's house, he made his deadly mark, Seventy brothers slain, in the dark.
Jotham, the youngest, snuck away, While Shechem crowned Abimelech that day.
Jotham stood on Gerizim, lifting his voice, "Listen up, Shechem, you made your choice.
"The trees sought a king: Olive said, 'I got my own, Why leave my oil, my rightful throne?'
"Fig tree said, 'My sweetness ain't for trade,' And the vine's new wine wasn't swayed.
"Then to the bramble, the trees turned, 'Come reign,' they asked, from wisdom they'd spurned.
"If truth you seek, shelter in my shade; Else fire will rise, make the cedars afraid.
"If Abimelech's your righteous king, then fine, But if not, let fire blaze, it's a dangerous line."
Jotham fled to Beer, fearing his kin's plot, Abimelech ruled three years, til the pot was hot.
God sent a rift, Shechem's men turned sly, For the blood of the seventy sons, justice would fly.
Ambush planned by the mountain's crest, Abimelech warned, Gaal put to the test.
Drunk in the field, Shechem cursed his name, Gaal challenged, "Abimelech's got no claim.
"Zebul's men? They're not my kin, Wish I led, I'd put him in a spin."
Zebul heard, boiling with rage, Crafted a message, set the stage.
"Gather by night, in the field lay," Abimelech struck at the break of day.
Gaal saw the shadows, thought them men, Zebul pushed him, "Fight, see where you've been."
Gaal fell back, Shechem lost hope, Zebul kicked him out, his brothers couldn't cope.
Abimelech split his forces, the city they took, Killed, salted the land, destruction shook.
Men of Shechem hid in fear of his reign, Abimelech burned the tower, their efforts in vain.
On to Thebez, another city in sight, But a woman from the tower put up a fight.
A millstone flew, busted his head, He called a young man, "Strike me dead.
Let no one say a woman did me in," So the young man complied, ending his spin.
When Israel saw Abimelech's demise, They scattered home, no surprise.
God repaid Abimelech's violent spree, Jotham's curse fulfilled, justice came to be.
After Abimelech, Tola arose, Issachar's son, In Shamir of Ephraim, his work was done.
For twenty-three years, he judged and then passed, In Shamir, he was buried, his legacy cast.
Next came Jair, Gilead's pride and joy, Judged for twenty-two years, a righteous envoy.
Thirty sons on donkey colts, thirty cities they claim, Havvoth Jair, their land, now known by that name.
Jair's life ended, Kamon his rest, But Israel's troubles were far from addressed.
They turned to Baals, Ashtaroth, gods galore, From Moab to Ammon, they worshipped more.
Yahweh's anger burned hot, and He let them fall, Philistines and Ammonites answered the call.
Eighteen years of oppression, Israel's plight, Across Jordan, Judah, and Benjamin, a constant fight.
In distress, they cried out, "Oh Yahweh, we see, We've sinned, and now we plea!"
Yahweh replied, "Didn't I save you before? From Egypt, Ammon, Philistines, and more?
Yet you turned, left Me for false gods' charms, Cry to them now, let them hold you in their arms!"
Israel cried, "We've sinned, do as you deem fit, But save us now, don't let our hope split."
They cast away idols, turned back to the Lord, Yahweh's heart ached, His love was restored.
Ammon gathered in Gilead, ready for war, Israel assembled, seeking a leader to restore.
The princes asked, "Who'll fight this fight? Lead us to victory, bring us to the light."
Jephthah the Gileadite, a mighty man of fame, Born to a prostitute, but he made his own name. Brothers pushed him out, said, "You can't stay, You're not one of us, go away today."
He fled to Tob, gathered outlaws, a crew, Living on the edge was all they knew. Then Ammon came to war, Gilead was in need, The elders called for Jephthah to take the lead.
"Be our chief, fight Ammon, take the throne," He answered, "You drove me out, left me alone. Why call me now when trouble's near? Do you think I'll just volunteer?"
But they swore, "Yahweh is witness, it's true, Lead us in battle, and we'll follow through." So Jephthah took the charge, made a vow, Before Yahweh in Mizpah, he spoke it loud.
He sent word to Ammon's king, "Why this fight? Claiming land from Egypt's flight isn't right." Ammon's king replied, "Return what you stole, Give back the land, make us whole."
Jephthah countered, "Israel took not your land, Passed through wilderness by Yahweh's hand." He recounted the history, laid it plain, "Your gods didn't help, but Yahweh reigns."
With Yahweh's Spirit, Jephthah crossed over, Made his vow, hoping to discover, "If Ammon's delivered, I'll give what's first seen, From my house door, be it clean."
He fought Ammon with God's aid and power, From Aroer to Minnith, they fell by the hour. Returning home, his daughter came out in dance, His only child, his heart felt a lance.
Tore his clothes, cried, "Daughter, my vow, Troubles me now, but I can't back down." She answered, "Father, do as you must, Yahweh's avenged us, in Him we trust."
Two months she mourned on the mountainside, With her friends, in grief did she bide. She returned, and the vow took its course, Her life given, a deep, solemn force.
And so it was, Israel's daughters each year, Honored Jephthah's daughter with a tear, Remembered the tale of courage and plight, Four days they sang, her memory in light.
Ephraim's crew gathered, marching with fire, "Jephthah, you left us out, now face our ire!"
Jephthah replied, "We were in a bind, I called for help, but you weren't inclined.
So I went alone, with no delay, Yahweh delivered them into my play.
Now you come to fight me today? Why the beef, what’s this display?"
Gilead and Ephraim clashed, fists in the air, Gilead struck hard, no mercy to spare.
At the Jordan's ford, they held the line, "Are you Ephraim?" they’d ask every time.
"Say 'Shibboleth,'" was the clever test, "Sibboleth," they'd stumble, wouldn’t pass the quest.
Seizing those who failed, at the river they'd fall, Forty-two thousand, Ephraim's mighty would stall.
Jephthah judged for six years, then he passed away, Buried in Gilead, his final stay.
Ibzan from Bethlehem took the lead, With thirty sons, daughters—quite a seed.
Seven years he judged, then he too was laid, In Bethlehem's earth, his dues were paid.
Elon of Zebulun then took the throne, Ten years he judged, his wisdom well-known.
Buried in Aijalon, in Zebulun’s land, His legacy carved by his quiet hand.
Abdon followed, with sons on donkeys they’d ride, Seventy colts strong, with familial pride.
Eight years he judged from Pirathon's core, In Ephraim's hills, he rests forevermore.
Israel's children did evil, forty years in plight, Philistines ruled, held them tight in their sight.
In Zorah's land, Manoah's wife was barren, childless, An angel appeared, brought news so timeless:
"You're childless now, but a son you'll conceive, No wine, no unclean, let this be your creed.
No razor shall touch, a Nazirite he'll be, To save Israel from Philistines, set them free."
She ran to Manoah, her heart full of awe, "An angelic face, the message I saw."
Manoah prayed, "O Lord, guide us again, Teach us, show us, for the child you ordain."
God heard Manoah, the angel returned, In the field to the woman, as Manoah yearned.
She dashed to her husband, "The man has appeared!" Manoah met the angel, his questions neared.
"Are you the one?" "I am," came the reply, "Let your words come true, tell us why."
The angel said, "Let her follow my command, No vine, no wine, let her understand."
Manoah offered, "A meal, stay a while," The angel declined, yet spoke with a smile.
"Offer to Yahweh, not food for me," Manoah, unknowing, agreed to the decree.
"What's your name?" Manoah did ask, "Incomprehensible," replied with no mask.
A goat was prepared, offered on the stone, The angel amazed them, rose in flame’s zone.
Manoah watched, both fell to the ground, Realized Yahweh's angel, truth profound.
"We'll surely die, we've seen God's face," But his wife assured, "We've found grace."
A son was born, Samson his name, He grew strong, Yahweh's Spirit aflame.
Between Zorah and Eshtaol, Spirit moved, Samson's path of destiny, God's strength proved.
Samson saw a girl in Timnah, a Philistine delight, Told his folks, "Get her for me, she feels so right." "Can't you find someone from our own line?" But Samson insisted, "She's the one, she's fine."
They didn’t know it was Yahweh's plan, Philistines ruling over the land, man. Down to Timnah with parents in tow, A lion roared, but Samson stole the show.
Spirit of Yahweh, mighty and bold, Tore the lion with hands, a story to be told. He kept it quiet, didn’t say a thing, Met the woman, his heart took wing.
Returned later, found bees and honey inside, Took some, shared it, but the source he’d hide. Samson threw a feast, as young men do, Thirty companions joined the crew.
He challenged them with a riddle to crack, "Answer right, get clothes, but if not, pay me back." "Out of the eater, food came to be, Out of the strong, came sweet as can be."
Days passed, they couldn’t get it right, Pressed his wife, "Get the answer tonight." She wept and pleaded, wore him down, On the seventh day, he finally came around.
She shared the secret, they solved the rhyme, "What’s sweeter than honey? Strong as a lion anytime?" "If you hadn't teamed with my heifer, You'd still be blind, see the weather."
Yahweh's Spirit filled him, rage burned fast, He struck thirty men, took their goods, a fierce blast. His anger fierce, to his father's he went, But his wife was given to his friend, his trust spent.

In the time of harvest, Samson came with a goat, To see his wife, but the father said, "No, you won't." "I thought you hated her, gave her to your friend, Her sister's more beautiful, take her instead, amend."

Samson replied, "This time I'm blameless when I fight, The Philistines will see my wrath, I'll set it right." He caught three hundred foxes, torches in between, Set them loose in fields, a fiery, furious scene.
Grain and groves burned up in the blazing light, Philistines asked, "Who'd do such a spite?" "Samson, son-in-law of the Timnite," they said, For taking his wife, now rage and fire spread.
Samson declared, "For this, revenge I'll take, Then I'll cease, but first, their lives I'll break." He struck them down, a great slaughter rose, Then he retreated to the Etam's rock to doze.
Philistines encamped, in Judah spread wide, "Why come against us?" Judah's men cried. "We're here for Samson, to bind him tight, To repay him for setting our fields alight."
Three thousand of Judah went to Samson's abode, "Philistines rule us, why bring this load?" "As they've done to me, so I’ve done to them," "Bind me, but harm me not, my own men."
"We'll bind you firm, deliver you," they swore, But not kill you, just settle the score. Bound in new ropes, up from the rock they led, To Lehi's land, where warriors tread.
Philistines shouted, ready for the fray, But God's Spirit came, tore the ropes away. With a donkey's jawbone, Samson laid waste, A thousand men fell, in a furious haste.
"With a jawbone, heaps on heaps," Samson's boast, "With a donkey's jaw, I've struck down their host." He tossed the bone aside, named the place then, Ramath Lehi, where he slayed many men.
Thirsty, he called, "Yahweh, will I now die, After this victory, in this land lie?" God split the ground, water flowed forth, Samson drank deep, his spirit renewed in worth.
He judged Israel in Philistine days, Twenty years of justice, in mighty ways.
Samson went to Gaza, saw a lady of the night, Word spread quick, "Samson's here, let's take him by surprise, tonight."
The Gazites lay in wait, quiet 'til the morning sun, "At dawn," they said, "we'll pounce, our victory begun."
But Samson, up at midnight, ready for some action, Tore the city gates, post and all, no distraction.
He put them on his shoulders, climbed to Hebron's top, Strong and bold, he didn't stop, he didn't flop.
Next, he loved Delilah in Sorek's valley wide, Philistines approached her, seeking secrets he would hide.
"Entice him," they said, "find his strength's source, Bind him, we'll pay you, follow this course."
Delilah asked Samson, "Tell me where your power lies," "If I'm bound with fresh cords, I'll be weak," he replies.
They tried the green cords, ambush set in the inner room, Samson broke them easy, while danger loomed.
"You've mocked me," Delilah cried, "tell me true," "If bound with new ropes, then weak I'll be too."
Again, he broke free, ropes couldn't hold, She pressed on further, growing bold.
"If you weave my hair with the fabric, then I'll fall," But he awoke, strong, and answered the call.
"How can you say you love me, when lies are all you give?" Day by day, she pressed, until his truth did relive.
"No razor's touched my head, a Nazirite I've been, Shave my head, my strength is gone, my weakness keen."
Seeing truth lay bare, she called her allies near, They shaved his head, his power disappeared.
"The Philistines are here, Samson!" she cried once more, But he was weak, Yahweh's strength no more.
The Philistines seized him, put out his eyes to blind, Bound him in bronze, in prison to grind.
Yet his hair began to grow, a silent sign of might, Philistines, in triumph, gave praise to Dagon's light.
"Our god has delivered Samson, our foe," they declared, Called him to perform, but underestimations were dared.
Samson said to the boy, "Let me feel the pillars strong," The house was full, three thousand looked on.
He prayed, "Lord Yahweh, remember me this day, Strengthen me once more, let the Philistines pay."
He pushed the pillars with all his power inside, "Let me die with them," he called, and with that, allied.
The house fell down, lords and people alike, More died in his death, avenged with his final strike.
His family came and took him, to bury him with care, In Manoah's site, twenty years his justice did declare.
In the hills of Ephraim lived a man named Micah, He told his mom, "I took your silver, now let's make it right, yah."
His mom blessed him, "May Yahweh's favor come," "I'll give the silver back, now let's get something done."
She dedicated the silver with a plan in her head, For a carved image and molten, she said.
Micah returned the cash, and she took a slice, Gave it to a silversmith, made idols nice.
Micah's house of gods was filling fast, He crafted an ephod, built a worship that would last.
No king in Israel, folks did what they pleased, Everyone living their life with ease.
From Bethlehem Judah, came a Levite young and bold, Traveling to find a place to unfold.
Micah asked, "From where do you come?" The Levite replied, "Bethlehem Judah's my home."
Micah said, "Stay with me, be my priest, wear my cloth, Ten silver pieces yearly, food and clothing, no froth."
The Levite agreed, content in his spot, Like a son to Micah, loving what he got.
Micah made it official, the Levite his guide, In Micah's house, the priest would abide.
Then Micah declared with hope so loud, "Yahweh's blessings are guaranteed; with a Levite, I'm proud."
In the days when no king led, Danites sought land to tread, Inheritance elusive still, so they sent heroes with skill.
Five men from Zorah set to roam, to spy and claim a home, "Go explore," their kin said loud, till they reached Micah's crowd.
They knew a voice, a Levite keen, asked, "Who brought you to this scene?" "I'm a priest for hire," he said, "Micah's house is where I'm led."
"Consult God for us," they pled, "We seek success ahead." "Go in peace," the priest replied, "Yahweh's favor's on your side."
To Laish these five men went, found a land without torment, Safe, secure, no ruler's sway, far from Sidon, lone to stay.
Back they rushed to brothers bold, "The land is good as gold. Arise, no time to waste, it's wide, and ours to take with pride."
The Danites armed and ready, marched on, six hundred steady, Camped in Judah for a night, then onward, hearts alight.
"Do you know in Micah's place, lie treasures, idols, and grace?" Five men whispered this clue, "Consider what you must now do."
To Micah's house they came once more, with weapons at the door, Took the ephod, teraphim, images carved and grim.
"What are you doing?" the priest implored, "Join us," they said, "and be adored.
"Hold your peace, come be our guide, a priest for tribe and kin abide." The priest agreed, glad with choice, took the treasures, joined their voice.
They took off with treasures in tow, leaving Micah in sorrow. Micah rallied but couldn't win, against Dan's might he could not begin.
"You stole my gods and priest," he cried, "What’s left for me inside?" Danites warned, "Hold your tongue, or meet angry men among."
Realizing their strength too grand, Micah returned to his own land. To Laish went Dan's fierce band, took the city with sword in hand.
They burned it down, no rescue came, built anew and changed its name. Named it Dan for lineage's pride, once Laish, now their side.
They set up Micah's image high, with priests to lead and not defy, Till Shiloh's house held God's might, the image stood in Dan’s sight.
In the days when Israel had no king to abide, A Levite took a concubine for his side. Out of Bethlehem Judah, she fled away, To her father's house, she went to stay.
Four months passed, her husband came to plead, With donkeys and a servant, to meet her need. Her father welcomed him, with joy in his face, Three days they ate, drank, and took up space.
On the fourth day, morning came, he sought to go, “Stay for bread,” the father said, “tarry slow.” They sat, they ate, the father urged with cheer, “Stay the night, make your heart merry here.”
The man rose to leave, the dawn of day five, “Stay 'til evening,” the father did strive. But the Levite, his heart set to roam, Refused the stay, sought his way home.
Near Jebus, as the sun began to set, The servant suggested they go in and rest. But the master pushed on, "Not here, not with these, To Gibeah we'll go, on the road with ease."
In Gibeah, they sat in the street, No one offered them a place to retreat. An old man from Ephraim, working late, Saw them there and joined their fate.
“Where do you travel? From where do you hail?” “From Bethlehem Judah, on Yahweh's trail. No one has taken us in, yet we lack no need, Straw, fodder, bread and wine, all we feed.”
The old man said, “Peace be upon your way, Come to my house, where you can stay.” They ate, drank, made merry through the night, When wicked men came, with evil in sight.
“Bring out the man,” they wickedly shout, The master pleaded, “Don't carry this out! Take my daughter, his concubine instead, But spare this man, leave this dread.”
They wouldn't listen, seized the woman by force, Abused her all night without remorse. At dawn she fell by the Levite's door, Her hands on the threshold, her spirit no more.
“Get up,” he said, but her silence was grave, He placed her on the donkey, to home he gave. In his house, with a heart filled with grief, He cut her body, piece by piece.
Sent twelve parts throughout the land, A message of horror, a call to stand. “All who saw it proclaimed with fear, No such deed had been done, or heard here.”
Israel gathered, a mighty scene, from Dan to Beersheba, all keen, In Mizpah they met, standing as one, four hundred thousand strong with sword drawn.
Benjamin heard of Israel's rise, asking, “What caused this despise?” The Levite spoke, his voice did quake, “In Gibeah, my concubine they did take.”
“They aimed to kill, surrounded our place, they harmed her and left disgrace. I sent her parts through Israel's land, a call for justice—take a stand!”
Israel vowed as one to fight, “We won't return home 'til we make it right. Against Gibeah we'll cast the lot, ten men per hundred to gather a plot.”
They sought Benjamin, demanded the men, “Give up the wicked, make peace again!” But Benjamin stood, refusing the plea, they prepared for battle, fierce as can be.
Israel's swords four hundred thousand in hand, Benjamin's twenty-six thousand did stand. “Who fights first?” they asked the sky, “Judah,” Yahweh answered, “let them try.”
Israel rose at dawn's first light, to face Benjamin, prepared for the fight. Gibeah's men did fierce attack, twenty-two thousand Israelites fell back.
Israel's tears flowed, they cried to the Lord, “Shall we fight again?” And He gave the word. They faced Benjamin, again they did meet, but eighteen thousand more faced defeat.
Then Israel fasted, wept in despair, and offered sacrifices with heartfelt prayer. “Shall we continue, or give up the fight?” “Go on,” said Yahweh, “I'll give you the night.”
With ambush set, they moved with stealth, against Gibeah, they crept with health. Benjamin struck, thinking they'd won, but Israel's plan had just begun.
The ambush rose, smoke filled the air, Benjamin turned and saw despair. With Israel's might, Benjamin's fall, twenty-five thousand in total, that was all.
Now Benjamin fled, but Israel pursued, surrounding them, their strength renewed. Eighteen thousand fell, valor in vain, the rest fled, seeking shelter from pain.
To the rock of Rimmon, six hundred fled, while their cities burned, Israel's anger spread. In fire and fury, they left no stone, bringing justice, their message shown.
In Mizpah, Israel made a vow, "No daughters to Benjamin, not now." In Bethel, voices raised, tears were shed, "God, why is one tribe's future dead?"
They built an altar, offerings burned bright, Asked, "Who didn't come to Yahweh's sight?" Mizpah's oath was a heavy load, Those absent faced death's harsh code.
Israel wept for Benjamin, their kin, "A tribe's cut off, how to begin? No daughters to give, what can we do? Find who missed the assembly view."
Jabesh Gilead, not a soul came through, Counted heads, none in the crew. Valiant men, twelve thousand strong, "To Jabesh, right the wrong."
"Strike with the sword," they did declare, Destruction left no one there. Four hundred maidens found alive, To camp Shiloh, they did arrive.
Peace to Benjamin, at Rimmon's rock, Brought the women, yet still in shock. The tribe broken, a breach in the land, Elders questioned, made their stand.
"An inheritance must stay, Benjamin's name, But our daughters can't join the claim." A plan was hatched, a feast at Shiloh, Daughters danced, and men lay low.
"Watch the vineyards, catch your bride, When fathers protest, we'll provide. Say, 'Not taken by battle's might, Nor given, so you stay right.'"
Benjamin moved, took the chance, Found wives among Shiloh's dance. Back to their land, cities rebuilt, Each tribe departed, paths were split.
No king ruled in those days, Each did right in their own ways.
Famine struck the land; from Bethlehem he went away / Elimelech took his wife and sons to Moab to stay
Elimelech died; his sons took Moabite wives / Orpah and Ruth, who became part of their lives
Ten years passed; both sons died, their Moab years done / Her husband and children were gone, every one
She heard Yahweh had given his people bread / With both daughters-in-law, toward Judah she sped
“Go home; may Yahweh repay kindness, grant rest in husbands’ homes” / They wept: “No, but we will return with you, to your people we’ll roam”
“Could sons in my womb wed you? Yahweh’s hand is against me” / “Orpah went back to her people and god; Ruth stayed with Naomi”
“Where you go, I’ll go; where you stay, I’ll stay; your people are mine” / “Your God, my God; where you die, I'll die, buried; death can part our line”
Naomi saw Ruth’s resolve and urged her no more / Together they reached Bethlehem; their journey was o’er
The townsfolk asked, “Is this Naomi?” as they drew near / “Call me Mara; the Almighty’s hand was severe”
“I went out full; Yahweh brought me home empty again” / “He accused me, afflicted me; barley harvest began”
Naomi’s husband’s kinsman, of Elimelech’s clan / Boaz was his name, a mighty and wealthy man
Ruth asked to glean behind him, where she might find favor that day / Naomi said, “Go, my daughter,” and sent her on her way
Ruth gleaned in Boaz’s field; he came from Bethlehem that day / He said, “May Yahweh be with you”; “May Yahweh bless you,” they’d say
Boaz asked his servant who the woman was in the field / “The Moabite back with Naomi, gleaning since morning,” he revealed
“Stay close among my maidens; don’t leave this field, just stay near” / “I’ve charged the young men not to touch you; drink water they’ve drawn here”
She bowed: “Why show me favor, a foreigner, with care?” / He heard deeds; may Yahweh grant full reward; His wings your refuge there
Boaz invited her to eat with the reapers and share / She ate until satisfied, and kept some food to spare
Boaz told men, “Let her glean among sheaves; don’t reproach her today” / “Pull grain from the bundles; leave it”; she gleaned till close of day
Ruth brought the grain home, told Naomi, “I worked for Boaz,” she said / “May Yahweh bless him; His kindness forsakes not living nor dead”
She had stayed with Boaz’s maidens through the barley, and then the wheat / She lived with her mother-in-law till both harvests were complete
Naomi said, “Wash, anoint, dress; to the threshing floor you go” / “Wait till he lies; bare his feet; lie down; he’ll tell what to do”
She went down and did all Naomi told her that day / At heap’s end he lay; she softly bared his feet, then lay
At midnight Boaz woke and asked, “Who are you tonight?” / “I’m Ruth, your servant; spread your cloak; you’re near kin by right”
“Your latter kindness surpassed the first; no young men did you pursue” / “The whole town knows you’re worthy; I’ll do what you ask me to”
One kinsman is nearer than I; if he will, let him do / “If he will not, as Yahweh lives, I’ll do the duty for you”
She lay till morning, rose before the day was bright / He said, “Let none know she came here”; keep that out of sight
She then told Naomi what he did and what he said / He gave six barley measures: “Don’t go empty to her,” he said
Naomi said, “Wait, daughter, till you know what happens; stay” / “Boaz won’t rest until he settles this today.”
Boaz meets the nearer kin beside the city gate / He calls ten elders, seats them there to witness the debate
Boaz says that Naomi sells Elimelech’s land / He offers first right; “I will redeem it,” says the man
He says, “You must buy Ruth too, the dead man’s wife” / “To raise his name upon the land, so it survives”
He will not risk his own inheritance; declines the right / He gives it to Boaz, removes his sandal to seal the rite
“I bought what Elimelech and his sons possessed” / “Ruth too, to be my wife, that dead man’s name not be suppressed”
“We witness; may she, like Rachel and Leah, build Israel’s house” / “May Perez’s house be yours, with offspring Yahweh gives as well”
Boaz marries Ruth; Yahweh enables her to conceive / She bears a son, whom Naomi will then receive
The women bless Yahweh; Naomi’s near kinsman is here / He’ll restore her life and sustain her through old years
Naomi takes the child and becomes his nurse there / Her neighbors name him Obed, David’s forebear
In Ramathaim Zophim, a man named Elkanah, Two wives he had, Hannah and Peninnah. Peninnah bore children, but Hannah was bare, Yearly they'd worship in Shiloh, offering each share.
Elkanah to Peninnah and her kids did provide, But to Hannah, his love, a double portion beside. Though Yahweh closed her womb, Peninnah would tease, Hannah wept bitterly, her heart never at ease.
Elkanah asked, "Hannah, why is your heart sore? Am I not better than ten sons and more?" But Hannah prayed deeply, tears flowed like a stream, Promised a son to God, if He'd fulfill her dream.
Eli the priest saw her lips move without sound, Thought she was drunk, but no drink was around. She pleaded, "I'm pouring my soul, not filled with wine, Out of pain and sorrow, I utter each line."
Eli said, "Go in peace; may God grant your choice." Her heart felt lighter, hope found its voice. They worshiped at dawn, to Ramah they trod, Elkanah and Hannah, blessed by God.
Time passed, Hannah conceived, a son she bore, Named him Samuel, "Asked of Yahweh," she swore. Elkanah went to make his vow, true and sincere, But Hannah said, "I'll wait till our child is clear."
Elkanah agreed, "Do what you deem right, May Yahweh's word stand firm in His sight." When Samuel was weaned, to Shiloh they came, With offerings in hand, to honor God's name.
Hannah spoke to Eli, "Remember me here? I prayed for this child, my words sincere. Now I give him to Yahweh, for all his days, To serve and worship, in all of his ways."
Hannah prayed with a heart full of joy, In Yahweh she found strength, no one could destroy. "My mouth's wide with triumph, my foes in retreat, In Your salvation, my heart skips a beat.
No one holy like Yahweh, no rock like our Lord, Proud words are empty, let humility be stored. Yahweh's knowledge weighs every act, Mighty bows break, while the weak gain tact.
Those once full, now work for their bread, The hungry are fed, the barren has spread. Yahweh brings life and takes it away, He humbles and lifts, come what may.
From dust to thrones, the needy He lifts, Raising them high with royal gifts. For the earth's pillars belong to Yahweh’s might, The wicked in darkness, silenced from sight.
Those who clash with Yahweh will shatter and fall, He thunders on high, His justice for all. Strength to His king, His anointed He'll raise, Elkanah returned home, giving God the praise.
But Eli's sons were wicked, they knew not the Lord, Priests taking the offerings they could not afford. With forks they took, not waiting their turn, Despising God's gifts, they refused to learn.
Yet Samuel served, clothed in linen fine, With a robe from his mother, year after year in line. Eli blessed them, praying for more, Yahweh answered, giving children galore.
Eli's sons sinned, he heard of their deeds, Sleeping with women, ignoring his pleas. "Why commit sins, bringing shame to our name?" But they ignored him, seeking no change.
A man of God came with a message so stark, "Didn't I choose you, give you a mark? Why disrespect My offerings, choosing your kin? Now, far be it from Me, for you've let sin in.
Your house will fall, no old man will last, Sorrow will come, your glory will pass. Hophni and Phinehas, in one day will die, I’ll raise a priest true, under My eye.
Those left will bow, seeking bread and plea, For honor and hope in My presence to be."
Young Samuel served before Yahweh's own, Eli old, with vision nearly gone.
Rare were visions, God's word was still, In the temple, God’s lamp hadn't gone nil.
Samuel laid where the ark had its place, Yahweh called out in the quiet space.
"Here I am," Samuel ran to Eli’s side, "I didn't call," Eli replied, "let it slide."
Once more, "Samuel!" the call was clear, Again to Eli, "I didn't call, my dear."
Samuel knew not Yahweh's voice yet, But Eli perceived what Samuel met.
Eli advised, "Next time, just say, 'Speak, Yahweh; your servant hears today.'"
Yahweh called, "Samuel! Samuel!" He said, "Speak; for your servant hears," Samuel pled.
"Behold," said Yahweh, "a thing I shall do, Israel will tingle when they hear it too.
Against Eli's house, it's all set to unfold, The iniquity known, the truth must be told."
Samuel lay till dawn, afraid to share, Eli called, "My son, what did Yahweh declare?"
"Tell me all, hide nothing from my view," Samuel told it all, Eli knew it was true.
"It is Yahweh, let Him do what's best," Samuel grew, God’s words he possessed.
From Dan to Beersheba, all knew the name, Samuel, a prophet, in Yahweh's fame.
Yahweh returned, in Shiloh’s light, Revealed to Samuel, God's word in sight.

Samuel spoke, Israel listened, ready for war, Against the Philistines, camped by Ebenezer's door. The Philistines stood tall, ready for the fight, Israel went down hard, four thousand lost that night.
Back at camp, elders cried, "Why this defeat? Let’s fetch Yahweh's ark, bring victory on our feet." To Shiloh they sent, for the ark of His might, With Eli’s sons, they brought it back in sight.
When the ark arrived, Israel shouted loud, The earth shook, echoing the proud. Philistines heard and trembled in fear, "The ark of God is here!" they cried, “Woe, oh dear!”

“They struck Egypt once, can we withstand their power? We must fight strong, this is our hour!” So they braced for battle, with courage they fought, Israel fled, thirty thousand lives there were caught.
The ark was seized, Eli’s sons fell, A messenger ran, their fate to tell. Eli sat waiting, heart tense with dread, Hearing news of the ark, he fell and was dead.
Phinehas' wife, near birth, heard the news, Her husband gone, she had much to lose. She gave birth and named her child with a sigh, Ichabod, “God’s glory has left,” was her cry.
"The glory has departed," she whispered, forlorn, For the ark was lost, leaving Israel torn.
The Philistines took the ark, brought it to Ashdod's land, Placed it next to Dagon, their idol, grand.
Morning came, Ashdod folks rose to see, Dagon facedown, a sight of mystery.
They picked him up, set him right once more, But next morning, same fate as before.
Dagon lay broken, head and hands on the floor, Only his body left by the door.
Priests of Dagon feared, the threshold they'd shun, Yahweh's power on Ashdod—none could outrun.
Yahweh’s hand was heavy, tumors struck them down, Ashdod’s borders trembled, fear spread through the town.
Men of Ashdod said, “This ark can't stay, His hand is fierce, we must send it away.”
Philistine lords gathered, seeking what to do, “Send it to Gath,” they decided, “Let it pass through.”
In Gath it went, but trouble followed still, Yahweh’s hand struck again, with a painful chill.
Tumors on the people, small and great, Confusion and cries, sealing their fate.
They sent the ark to Ekron, but the cries began, “They’ve brought the ark to kill us, to kill every man!”
Philistine lords convened, troubled with dread, “Send it back home, or we’ll all end up dead.”
Panic in the city, God’s hand heavy and grim, Those left alive, prayed and cried out to Him.
Seven months Philistines had the ark in their land, Calling priests and diviners to lend a hand,
"What to do with Yahweh's ark?" they asked, "Where to send it, what's the task?"
"Don't send it empty, give a trespass fee, Five golden tumors, and mice there'll be."
For the lords of Philistine, for the plague on you all, Images to glorify Israel's God so tall.
"Don't harden your hearts like Pharaoh's crew, Release His hand, let it not trouble you."
"Prepare a new cart, two cows without yoke, Tie them there, separate calves—no joke."
Place the ark on the cart, the gold by its side, Send it on its way, let Yahweh guide.
"If it finds its border, Beth Shemesh ahead, Then it's He who brought this dread."
So the men took the cows, tied them with care, Put the ark on the cart, offering to bear.
Cows headed straight, lowing all the way, Philistine lords followed, in dismay.
Beth Shemesh folk harvesting in the field, Eyes lifted, saw the ark revealed.
The cart stopped in Joshua's land so wide, Wood split, cows sacrificed, nothing to hide.
Levites took the ark, placed it on the stone, Offered sacrifices, worship shown.
Philistine lords saw and went back home, Ark returned, and the message was known.
Golden tumors, golden mice, cities all aligned, To the great stone where Yahweh's ark reclined.
But they peeked inside, Beth Shemesh men, Yahweh struck them, mourning began.
"Who can stand before this holy God?" they cried, "To whom shall the ark go?" they sighed.
They called Kiriath Jearim folks, "Come here, The Philistines returned the ark, come take it near."
The men of Kiriath Jearim came real quick, Took Yahweh's ark, up the hill, it was slick. Into Abinadab’s house, it found its rest, Eleazar consecrated, to guard it with zest.
For twenty long years, the ark stayed in place, Israel lamented, seeking Yahweh’s grace. Samuel spoke up, to Israel's hearts, "Turn to Yahweh, that's where it starts.
Put away idols, serve Him alone, He’ll deliver you, make His power known." Israel listened, cleared out the old, Served Yahweh only, their faith emboldened.
Samuel called, "Meet me at Mizpah's gate, I'll pray to Yahweh, let's set things straight." They gathered, they fasted, water poured down, Confessed their sins, as Samuel wore the crown.
Philistines heard, they gathered with might, Israel feared, in the looming fight. They pleaded with Samuel, "Cry out to our God, To save us from their threatening squad."
Samuel took a lamb, offered it whole, Cried to Yahweh, pouring out his soul. As the Philistines neared, ready for war, Yahweh thundered loudly, shook them to the core.
Israel chased them, struck them down hard, Pushed them back, 'neath Beth Kar's guard. Samuel set a stone, Ebenezer its name, "Yahweh helped us," they all proclaimed.
Philistines subdued, stopped crossing the line, Yahweh's hand held firm, in Samuel's time. Cities restored, peace with Amorites, Samuel judged, through days and nights.
Yearly he traveled, Bethel to Mizpah round, Judgment and justice in every town found. Back to Ramah, his home so dear, Built an altar to Yahweh, year by year.
Samuel got old, his sons took the stand, But they strayed from his path, corrupted the land. In Beersheba they judged, but they chased after gold, Took bribes, twisted justice, breaking the mold.
Israel's elders came, gathered in Ramah's town, "You're old, your sons fail, so bring us a crown. Make us like others, a king on the throne," But Samuel was troubled, felt all alone.
He prayed to Yahweh, seeking His say, Yahweh spoke clear, "Listen, don't dismay. They reject not you, but me as their King, Since Egypt they've turned, now doing this thing.
Hear their demand, but make sure they know, The king's heavy hand, how his power will grow." Samuel warned them, spoke Yahweh's decree, "The king will take sons, for his chariots they'll be.
Captains and soldiers, harvesting lands, Crafting his weapons, working with hands. Daughters for perfume, baking, and more, Fields and vineyards, he'll take and store.
A tenth of your seed, vineyards and fruit, To officers, servants, he'll recruit. Your servants and flocks, he'll claim as his own, You'll be his servants, your freedoms overthrown.
You'll cry out loud, for the king you chose, But Yahweh won't hear, you'll reap what you sow." Yet the people refused, their hearts were set, "We want a king, like the others, no regret.
To judge us, to lead, to fight our fight," Samuel took their words, repeated them right. Yahweh said, "Let them have their way, Give them a king, as they say."
Samuel sent them all back to their home, Israel would have a king, not alone.
In the land of Benjamin, Kish was the man, A mighty dude with a courageous plan. His son was Saul, tall and grand, No one like him in all the land.
Kish's donkeys roamed and strayed, "Saul," he said, "go, find where they've laid." Through Ephraim's hills, they made their way, Searched Shalishah, Shaalim, no luck that day.
In Zuph, Saul said, "Let's head home, Dad will worry, left alone." But the servant said, "Hold up, bro, A man of God nearby, let's ask where to go."
Saul replied, "What can we bring? Our bread is gone, got not a thing." The servant showed a silver piece, "Let's give this, and gain some peace."
"Good plan," said Saul, "let's track him down," Maidens said, "The seer's in town." They hurried on, with hope in sight, Found Samuel before the night.
God spoke to Sam the day before, "From Benjamin, I'll send one more. Anoint him prince, he'll lead the fight, Against Philistines, with might and right."
Saul met Sam at the city's gate, "Where's the seer?" he asked, not late. Samuel said, "You're eating with me, Tomorrow, all you need, you'll see."
"Don't stress the donkeys, they're back home, Israel's riches are yours alone." Saul said, "But I'm just a Benjamite, The smallest tribe, why this delight?"
Samuel set them in the place of honor, Thirty gathered, as they pondered. The cook brought forth the special meat, Saved for Saul, now ready to eat.
On the rooftop, they talked till dawn, Samuel called, "Time to move on." At the city's edge, Sam took pause, "Send the servant, hear God's cause."
As Saul stood still, the message clear, The journey began with no more fear.
Samuel poured the oil, let it drip and glide, Kissed his head, said, "You're the prince, no need to hide.
When you leave me, find two men by Rachel's tomb, They'll say, 'The donkeys are found, and your dad's in gloom.'
Head to Tabor's oak, three men you'll greet, Goats, bread, and wine they carry, gifts so sweet.
They'll hand you loaves, just take it, no fight, Next stop, God's hill, where prophets ignite.
You'll join in with music, a lute, a tambourine, Spirit of Yahweh strong, you'll see what I mean.
You'll prophesy with them, be changed inside, God's spirit with you, no need to hide.
"Go to Gilgal, wait for me there, In seven days, I'll show you with care."
Saul turned away, with a heart brand new, Prophets met him, God's spirit flew.
People asked, "Is Saul a prophet too?" Confused, they wondered, "What's he gonna do?"
Uncle inquired, "Where have you been?" Saul replied, "Off to find donkeys again."
He kept the kingdom talk hidden away, Samuel gathered the tribes for Yahweh's say.
"You asked for a king, rejected God above, Now stand before Yahweh, show him your love."
Benjamin was chosen, Saul was the one, But he hid in the baggage, avoiding the sun.
They found him there, taller than the rest, Samuel said, "See the one Yahweh's blessed?"
People cheered, "Long live the king!" they cried, Samuel wrote the rules, then sent them aside.
Saul went home, with followers true, But some doubted, "What can this guy do?"
Yet Saul held his peace, with patience he stood, While Yahweh's plan unfolded as it should.
Nahash the Ammonite came to Jabesh's gate, Men of Jabesh pleaded, “Serve you, if you let us relate.”
Nahash replied, “Only if your right eyes are torn, I’ll disgrace all Israel, leave them forlorn.”
Jabesh elders said, “Give us seven days to see, If no help arrives, we’ll bow to your decree.”
Messengers ran to Gibeah, spoke to the crowd, Tears filled their eyes, weeping so loud.
Saul came from the field, asked, “Why the cries?” Heard Jabesh's plight, anger did rise.
God’s Spirit filled Saul, his rage did ignite, He cut oxen in pieces, sent them in the night.
“Come after Saul, follow Samuel’s call, Or your oxen will suffer, the same fate befall.”
Fear of Yahweh united them, as one they did stand, Three hundred thousand with Judah’s mighty band.
Messengers said, “Jabesh, rescue comes ‘morrow, By the sun’s heat, no more sorrow.”
Jabesh replied, “Tomorrow, we’ll come out to you, Do what seems good; let’s see what you’ll do.”
At dawn Saul divided them, three companies strong, Struck the Ammonites, battles did throng.
By noon’s heat, the foe scattered far and wide, No two together, nowhere to hide.
Voices rose, “Who doubted Saul’s reign? Bring them here, let them feel the pain!”
Saul declared, “No death today, Yahweh has saved Israel in a mighty way.”
Samuel said, “To Gilgal, let’s renew the crown,” There they made Saul king, peace offerings went down.
In Gilgal, joy echoed, sacrifices laid, Saul and Israel rejoiced, a kingdom remade.
Samuel stepped up, addressed the crowd, "I've heard your cries, and made you proud. A king now walks before your eyes, I'm old and gray, but wise, I advise.
Witness now, before the Lord and king, Did I take your ox, your donkey, anything? Did I defraud, oppress, or take a bribe? If so, I'll restore and make it right."
"You've done us no wrong," the people said, "Yahweh's witness, let it be spread." Samuel reminded, "Moses, Aaron too, Led you out of Egypt, remember their view.
But once you forgot, God let foes reign, Sisera, Philistines, Moab's claim. You cried out, confessed sins and plea, God sent Jerubbaal, Bedan, and me.
When Nahash came, you sought a king, Though Yahweh was your everything. Behold the king you chose in haste, But honor God, or face disgrace.
Stand still, and watch this mighty scene, It's wheat harvest, the sky will glean. I'll call to Yahweh, thunder will roll, To show how your wickedness takes its toll."
Samuel called, and thunder did roar, Rain poured down, fear struck their core. "Pray for us, Samuel!" the people cried, "To Yahweh, lest we die inside."
"Fear not, though you've done wrong, Stay with Yahweh, keep your hearts strong. Don't chase after things that won't fulfill, Yahweh’s with you, He loves you still.
I'll keep praying, teach you His way, Fear Yahweh truly, let your heart obey. Consider His deeds, so mighty, so grand, But stray into evil, and you'll lose this land."
Saul at thirty took the throne, Israel's king, Forty-two years, he'd let his reign swing. Three thousand troops, he chose his own, Two thousand with him, where Michmash was shown.
Jonathan in Gibeah, a thousand by his side, Struck the Philistines, their presence defied. Saul blew the trumpet, a rallying sound, “Let the Hebrews hear!” he declared all around.
Israel heard, the Philistines were vexed, With hatred, they gathered, ready and perplexed. Thirty thousand chariots, horsemen galore, Like sands by the sea, they prepared for war.
Seeing danger, Israel's men in distress, Hid in caves, thickets, rocks, in their stress. Some crossed to Gad, while Saul stayed in place, In Gilgal, trembling, they gathered with haste.
Seven days waited, but Samuel was late, People scattered, fearing their fate. Saul said, “Bring the offerings near,” He offered burnt offerings, trembling with fear.
Just as he finished, Samuel appeared, Saul went to greet him, but what he feared neared. “What have you done?” Samuel asked with a frown, Saul explained why he laid the offering down.
“The people were leaving, you didn't arrive, Philistines gathered, I couldn't survive. So I made the offering, to seek Yahweh's grace.” Samuel replied, “You’ve left Yahweh’s embrace.
You acted foolishly, ignored God’s call, Your kingdom now destined to falter and fall. Yahweh has sought a heart after His own, A new prince appointed, for obedience shown.”
Samuel left, Saul counted men on hand, Six hundred stood firm, ready to withstand. In Geba, they camped, as Philistines closed, Three raider companies, their menace exposed.
No blacksmiths in Israel, Philistines' control, No swords or spears, only tools to console. Each man to the Philistines, to sharpen their gear, Plowshares and axes, all in disrepair.
On battle day, no weapons in sight, Only Saul and Jonathan prepared for the fight. Philistines at Michmash, their garrison set, The tension was high, the stage firmly met.
Jonathan whispers, "Let's roll to the Philistine's base, Keep it quiet, don't tell Dad, let's pick up the pace."
Saul's under a pomegranate tree, just chillin' with six hundred men, Ahijah the priest is with them, wearing the ephod again.
Jonathan and his armor bearer squeeze through rocky crags, Seneh and Bozez are their names, these rocks have their own tags.
Jonathan says, "Let's confront those uncircumcised, Yahweh's got no limits, many or few, we'll rise."
His armor bearer nods, "I'm with you, heart to heart, Let's go to those Philistines, let's play our part."
"If they call us to come, that's our sign, Yahweh's plan, If they come to us, we stay put, that's the way it’ll stand."
They showed themselves, Philistines mocked, "Come up, let's see, Jonathan climbs, armor bearer follows, with Yahweh's decree."
Jonathan slays, armor bearer cleans up, twenty men down, Tremors shake the ground, Philistines wear a frown.
Saul's lookout sees the chaos, "Who's missing? Do a call," Jonathan and his armor bearer, not with Saul.
"Bring the Ark," says Saul, the priest's hand withdraws, Philistines in confusion, it's time to hit 'em with force.
Hebrews in Philistine camp flip sides, Israelites from Ephraim's hills join the tide.
Yahweh saves the day, yet Saul's curse lies thick, No food till sunset, his rule's got a trick.
Honey drips in the woods, people fear the oath, Jonathan tastes, eyes bright, breaking the troth.
"Father's troubled the land," Jonathan cries, "If we had eaten, more Philistines would lie."
The folks are faint, pounce on plunder, Eating with blood, Saul's anger starts to thunder.
"Roll a stone," he cries, "Eat right, don't sin, Kill at the altar, cleanse from within."
Saul plans a night raid, but God stays silent, "Let's find the sin," Saul says, determined and defiant.
Lot falls on Jonathan, who says with a sigh, "I tasted the honey, now I must die."
Saul declares, "You will surely fall," The people rise up, "No way, not at all!"
Jonathan saved from death by the people's plea, Philistines retreat, they set themselves free.
Saul fights all around, takes on every foe, Philistines, Moab, and more, wherever he'd go.
His sons, his daughters, his captains, they stand, But Saul's eyes always open for mighty men across the land.
Samuel approached Saul with Yahweh’s decree, "Listen now, you’re the king, anointed by me.
Remember Amalek and their old attack, Go destroy them all, leave nothing to come back."
Saul gathered troops, counted them all, Two hundred thousand strong, heeding the call.
To Amalek’s city, Saul set the scene, Ambushed the valley, his intent was keen.
To the Kenites he said, "Depart from their side, You showed us kindness, now go and hide."
Saul struck Amalek down, from Havilah to Shur, Spared Agag, but destruction was meant to be pure.
Kept the best cattle, the sheep and the lambs, Ignored God’s command, took riches in hands.
Yahweh’s word to Samuel, heavy with grief, Saul has turned, causing me disbelief.
Samuel confronted Saul, who claimed to obey, But sounds of livestock gave his words away.
Saul blamed the people, said they’d sacrifice, "But Yahweh prefers obedience over vice."
"Rebellion’s like witchcraft, stubbornness like sin, Since you rejected God, He’s rejecting your kin."
Saul admitted wrong, "I feared men, not the Lord, Please pardon my sin, to worship restore."
Samuel refused, "Yahweh’s word you did spurn, He’s torn the kingdom, you get no return."
Saul’s robe tore, as Samuel turned away, "The kingdom’s given to a better man today."
Saul pleaded again, "Honor me before my own, Come back with me, let my worship be known."
Samuel went with Saul, setting his face, Then Agag was brought, with deceptive grace.
Samuel spoke sharp, "Your sword made women cry, Now it’s your mother’s turn, and here you die."
Samuel cut Agag, judgment was swift, Both parted ways, in somber rift.
Samuel mourned, saw Saul nevermore, Yahweh grieved the king He once bore.
Samuel mourning, tears for Saul, God said, "Move on, I've made the call.
Fill your horn, take some oil, go to Jesse's place, Among his sons, a new king I'll embrace."
Samuel worried, "Saul will kill me if he knows." God replied, "Take a heifer, let the purpose be the shows."
"Call Jesse to the sacrifice, I'll guide your hand, Anoint the one I'll choose, as I've planned."
Samuel did as God commanded, reached Bethlehem's gate, Elders trembling, "Do you come in peace or with fate?"
"Peacefully," said Samuel, "Sanctify, prepare, Join the sacrifice, Jesse and sons, I'll see them there."
Eliab stood tall, Samuel thought he was the one, But God said, "Don't judge by looks, his heart's not won."
Abinadab passed by, but God shook his head, Then came Shammah, "Not this one," He said.
Seven sons presented, none were the king, Samuel asked, "Got any left? Let the youngest bring."
David tending sheep, summoned to the scene, Ruddy with handsome features, eyes keen.
God declared, "Arise! Anoint this one, he's the key." Samuel poured the oil, God's Spirit stirred mightily.
Saul's spirit troubled, an evil one near, His servants whispered, "Let's find peace, draw him near."
"Seek a harp player, skilled with the sound, To soothe Saul's spirit when the evil comes around."
One servant spoke, "Jesse's son, David's his name, A warrior, wise talker, with him God's flame."
Saul sent for David, a donkey loaded for the trip, Bread, wine, young goat, in Jesse's grip.
David stood before Saul, found in his eyes, Became armor bearer, winning favor, no disguise.
When the spirit troubled Saul, David played his harp’s grace, Saul felt refreshed, evil spirit erased.
Philistines gathered, armies ready for war, In Judah at Socoh, their battle roar. Saul and Israel camped in Elah’s field, Mountains on each side, neither side would yield.
Goliath stepped out, tall and fierce, Six cubits and a span, in bronze gear pierced. A helmet of bronze, mail weighing him down, Bronze on his legs, javelin renowned.

While with Moab's king, they found refuge strong, Gad the prophet spoke, "Judah is where you belong." David moved to Hereth, in the forest he stayed, Meanwhile Saul heard where David had laid.

David heard a shout, Philistines at Keilah's door, Threshing floors robbed, couldn't take it anymore.
He asked God, "Should I fight, should I strike?" God said, "Go save Keilah, it's time to hike."

Joab's men marched through the night, Back to Hebron, with dawn's first light.
In Hebron, David’s house grew strong and bold, While Saul’s house weakened, its story told.
David had sons, born one by one, Amnon, Chileab, Absalom, their life begun.
Adonijah, Shephatiah, Ithream too, In Hebron these sons of David grew.
Abner gained power, Saul’s house on his side, But Ishbosheth’s words made his anger rise wide.
“Am I a dog’s head with Judah’s crew? I’ve kept you safe, yet you question what I do!”
“God do more if I don't keep David’s throne, From Saul’s house, to rule from land to known.”
Abner sent word, “Let’s make this deal, Bring all Israel, for David’s appeal.”
David replied, “Make this treaty be, But bring Michal, and you’ll see me.”
Ishbosheth sent for her, took her away, Paltiel wept, but to Bahurim he’d stay.
Abner spoke to Israel, “David’s your king, Yahweh’s promise, salvation he’ll bring.”
Abner came to David with twenty men, And David feasted, peace reigned again.
Joab returned from a raid with his band, He learned Abner came, but left the land.
“What have you done?” Joab asked the king, “Abner’s deceit, he knows everything.”
Joab called Abner back, at the gate he did meet, Struck him down, for his brother's defeat.
David mourned, “I’m guiltless of this blood, Let Joab’s house bear the flood.”
“Clothe in sackcloth, mourn Abner this day,” David followed the bier, leading the way.
“Should Abner fall like a fool in the dust, With no bonds or chains, betrayed by unjust?”
David wept, the people joined the cry, He swore not to eat till the sun passed by.
The people saw and it pleased them right, The king’s heart was clear in their sight.
“A great man’s fallen, though I’m weak today, May Yahweh judge the wicked, for their wicked way.”
Saul's son heard of Abner's fall, His hands grew weak, his spirit small. Israel trembled, stricken with fear, Two raider captains were drawing near.
Baanah and Rechab, brothers in crime, From Beeroth's land, Benjamin's line. Jonathan's boy, young but lame, Mephibosheth was his name.
Rechab and Baanah, in the heat of the day, To Ishbosheth's house, they made their way. Pretended to fetch wheat, all was still, Struck him down as he lay in the chill.
In his bed, they took his breath, Killed and beheaded, sealing his death. They seized his head, off to David they sped, Through the night, in the Arabah, they tread.
To Hebron with Ishbosheth's head they came, "Here's Saul's son's head," they proclaimed. "Yahweh avenged you, King, this day, Saul's end is here," they dared to say.
David replied with a heart full of fire, “As Yahweh lives, my soul's true supplier, When news of Saul's death came to me, I rewarded the bearer with fatal decree.
Now you wicked men, who killed a just soul, In his own bed, you've paid the toll." David commanded, justice was set, Hands and feet cut, a grim silhouette.
Beside Hebron's pool, their fate was sealed, Ishbosheth's head, in Abner's field. David made sure it all was done, Justice served, the light of the sun.
All the tribes gathered, their voices were strong, "We're your bone and flesh, we've been here all along.
Back when Saul reigned, you led us in and out, Yahweh said, 'You'll lead, of that there's no doubt.'
Elders came to Hebron, in front of Yahweh they stood, With a covenant made, David's rule was understood.
Thirty years young, he began his reign, Forty years on, his leadership plain.
Seven years and some months he ruled in Hebron's sight, Then thirty-three in Jerusalem, his kingdom bright.
To Jerusalem he marched, the Jebusites defiant, "The blind and lame will stop you," they were reliant.
Yet David took Zion, now called David's town, "Strike the blind and lame," he said, taking them down.
In his stronghold he lived, his city named, David built around, his greatness proclaimed.
With Yahweh on his side, David rose higher, Hiram of Tyre sent gifts to inspire.
Cedar, carpenters, and masons came along, A house for David, where he would belong.
He knew Yahweh's hand established him king, For Israel's sake, the praises they'd sing.
More concubines and wives, his family grew wide, Sons and daughters born, his legacy applied.
Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon fair, Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, Japhia there.
Elishama, Eliada, Eliphelet named, In Jerusalem, their heritage claimed.
Philistines heard of David, anointed and true, They sought him out, but he knew what to do.
Down to the stronghold David did go, The Philistines spread out, their numbers did grow.
"Shall I fight them, Yahweh?" David inquired, "Go up," said Yahweh, "their defeat is desired."
Baal Perazim, the battle was won, "Yahweh broke them like waters," David's shout was done.
They left their idols, to David's men they stayed, Philistines returned, but Yahweh's plan was laid.
"Circle behind, wait by the mulberry trees, When you hear them march, move with ease."
Yahweh led the charge, Philistines fell, From Geba to Gezer, David's story to tell.
David gathered thirty thousand, a chosen mighty band, To bring God's ark from Judah's land, a task so grand.
They set the ark on a cart, new and bright, Uzzah and Ahio drove it, guiding it right.
Instruments played, cypress wood, harps in hand, Tambourines, cymbals—music filled the land.
But at Nacon's floor, Uzzah reached out bold, The cattle stumbled, the ark's touch was cold.
God's anger burned, Uzzah fell, struck down, David, displeased, named the place with a frown.
"How can Yahweh's ark come to me?" David cried, Afraid, he left it, in Obed-Edom's house to abide.
For three months it stayed, blessings poured down, David heard the news, joy spread around the town.
He went to bring the ark, joyfully to his city, Six paces in, they sacrificed with heartfelt pity.
David danced with might, in linen ephod he spun, Shouting, trumpets blared, a celebration begun.
Michal watched from the window, despising the scene, As David danced before Yahweh, heart open and keen.
The ark found its place in a tent set with care, Burnt offerings, peace offerings, David's prayer.
To all the people, bread, dates, raisins as a feast, A blessing in Yahweh's name, joy increased.
Michal scorned, "How glorious today, your display!" But David replied, "Before Yahweh, I'd dance this way."
"I'll be more vile, in my own sight less, Yet the maids will honor me, my joy confess."
And Michal, childless, lived on through her days, As David danced on, giving Yahweh his praise.

The king sat at peace, his battles all done, Said to Nathan, "Look, I've got a house of cedar, son. But the Ark of God stays behind a curtain thin." Nathan said, "Do what's in your heart; Yahweh's with you within."
That night Yahweh spoke to Nathan clear, "Tell David, 'Should you build me a house here? I've roamed in tents since Egypt set them free, Did I ask for cedar walls surrounding me?
Remember David, where you came from, the sheep, I made you a prince, gave you enemies' defeat. I'll make your name great, like giants of old, Plant Israel firm, their story unfold.
I'll give them peace, their troubles will cease, And David, I'll build you a house in my lease. When your days are done, and you're laid to rest, Your offspring will rise, kingdom blessed.
He'll build for my name, his throne will last, I'll be his father, his future's cast. If he errs, he'll bear the human rod, Yet my love won't leave, unlike Saul's flawed.
Your house, your reign, forever secure, Your throne established, this promise is pure." Nathan told David every word, every sight, The king sat with Yahweh, in this divine light.
"Who am I, Lord Yahweh? What is my line? That you've brought me this far, in your grand design. This promise extends beyond what I see, You've chosen my house for eternity.
No words can express, for you know me well, Your greatness is clear, no story can tell. Israel redeemed, a people of your own, You made them a name, in lands they were shown.
Yahweh, confirm your word, let it be, Magnify your name, for all to see. You promised a house to stand evermore, Blessed be this house, forever in your lore."
David stepped up, struck the Philistine land, Took their city's power, wrested it from their hand.
He marched to Moab, with a line he measured, Two parts gone, one part kept, a decision he treasured.
Servants they became, tribute they brought, David's reign expanded, battles he fought.
Hadadezer of Zobah, next in line, David took his soldiers, claimed them as mine.
Seventeen hundred horsemen, twenty thousand on foot, Chariots hamstrung, a hundred he took.
Syrians of Damascus tried to lend aid, David struck twenty-two thousand, made them afraid.
Garrisons in Syria, they served him now, Tribute to David, Yahweh's gift, take a bow.
Golden shields from Hadadezer brought to town, Betah and Berothai's bronze made David renown.
Toi of Hamath, hearing of David's might, Sent his son Joram, with gifts shining bright.
Silver and gold, they arrived at his feet, David dedicated all to Yahweh, complete.
Nations he subdued, from Moab to Philistine, Ammon, Amalek, all he did oversee.
In the Valley of Salt, David's name became known, Eighteen thousand Syrians, his power was shown.
Edom secured, garrisons placed all around, The Edomites served, Yahweh's victory profound.
David ruled Israel with fairness and might, Justice and righteousness were his guiding light.
Joab, the commander, led with a strong hand, Jehoshaphat recorded the events of the land.
Zadok and Ahimelech were priests in the scene, Seraiah the scribe, keeping the records clean.
Benaiah over guards, the Cherethites and Pelethites, David’s sons as ministers, guiding people’s rights.
David wondered, "Is there anyone left from Saul's line? Jonathan's sake, I'm showing kindness, it's time to shine."
A servant named Ziba, from Saul's house, came near. "Are you Ziba?" the king asked. "Yes, I'm here."
"Is there anyone left from Saul's family, I pray? To show God's kindness, in a generous way?"
"Jonathan has a son," Ziba said, "though he's lame." "In Machir's house, Lo Debar, that's his name."
So King David sent for him, brought him from afar, From Machir's house, Lo Debar, under David's star.
Mephibosheth bowed low, respect on his face. David called, "Mephibosheth," in the king's place.
"Don't be afraid," David said, "kindness you'll see, For Jonathan's sake, your father's land, I decree.
At my table, you'll eat, bread without strife, Restored lands to you, a secure, honored life."
"What am I," he asked, "a dead dog you'd seek?" Yet David showed kindness to the humble and meek.
To Ziba, the king said, "All Saul had, it's done, For Mephibosheth, your master's son."
"Work the land, bring the harvest in hand, But Mephibosheth eats at my table, understand?"
Ziba agreed, with fifteen sons, twenty men, "All you command, I'll fulfill, again and again."
Mephibosheth dined, like a king's son, with pride, In Jerusalem, at the table, he'd abide.
His son Mica watched his father, glad to see, How kindness and grace from the king set him free.
Though lame in his feet, Mephibosheth's heart soared, For at David's table, he was always restored.

The king of Ammon passed, Hanun took his throne, David said, "I'll show kindness, the seed's been sown." Sent his servants to Hanun, in his grief to console, But Ammon's princes whispered, sowing doubt in the soul.

"Is David here to honor, or is it a spy game? Is he here to comfort or to claim Ammon's fame?" Hanun listened, took the servants, shaved half their beards, Cut their garments, sent them off in shame and fears.
Word reached David, he met them, saw their disgrace, "Stay in Jericho till your beards replace." Ammon saw they were foul in David's sight, Called Syrians for battle, gearing up for a fight.
David heard the news, sent Joab with the force, Ammon lined up at the gate in full course. Joab, seeing foes both front and back, Chose Israel's best, prepared for the attack.
"If Syrians press, then come lend me aid, If Ammon's too strong, I'll come with brigade. Be brave for our people, for the cities we hold, Let Yahweh decide what's good, what's bold."
Joab charged, Syrians fled from his sight, Ammon saw them run, took flight from the fight. Joab returned to the city, back home they trod, Syrians regrouped, plotting against the rod.
Hadadezer summoned forces, crossed the river wide, Shobach led with might, ready to collide. David gathered Israel, crossed Jordan's wide stream, Met Syrians in Helam, battle's brutal dream.
Syrians fled, David's strength held strong, Seven hundred charioteers, forty thousand gone. Struck down Shobach, their captain fell that day, Kings under Hadadezer saw defeat, turned away.
Peace they sought, with Israel they made, Syrians feared to help Ammon, with their aid they stayed.
In the springtime, when kings go to fight, David sent Joab, his army, a fearsome sight. They crushed Ammon and laid Rabbah under siege, But David stayed back, in Jerusalem’s peace.
One evening, restlessly he roamed his roof high, Saw a woman bathing, caught his eye. "Who is this beauty?" he asked with intent, "Bathsheba," they told him, "Uriah's wife, heaven-sent."
So David summoned her, and she came near, He knew her well, then she disappeared. Later she sent word, "I'm with child," David’s heart raced, his thoughts ran wild.
"Bring me Uriah," David decreed, Joab sent him back, fulfilling the need. David inquired of how Joab fared, "Go home, rest, let your worries be spared."
But loyal Uriah stayed by the gate, With servants he slept, his duty innate. David was puzzled, called him back too, "Why not go home, enjoy what’s due?"
"The ark, the troops, they’re in the fields," he pled, "I can’t enjoy comforts, while they shed." David persisted, "Stay one more day," Made Uriah drink, but firm he'd stay.
Next morning, David wrote with a heavy heart, Sent Uriah to Joab, played his part. "Put him upfront where the battle's hot, Then step back, leave him in that spot."
Joab obeyed, at the city’s edge, Uriah fell—war’s tragic pledge. News came to David, the report was grim, "Uriah's gone, others too, fallen victims."
David replied, "Let Joab press on, Strengthen the fight, until the city's gone." Bathsheba mourned, her tears were real, But soon joined David, a new life to feel.
Yet in this tale, God's displeasure reigned, David’s choices marked, consequences gained.

Nathan came to David, with a tale to unfold, About two men in a city, one rich, one with pockets cold. The rich man had flocks, more than he could ever need, The poor man just one lamb, his heart's only feed.
The lamb grew with him, like a daughter it stayed, A traveler came, and the rich man betrayed. He took the poor man's lamb, prepared it for the guest, David burned with anger, his fury didn't rest.
"As Yahweh lives," David shouted out, "The man who did this deserves to be knocked out. Restore the lamb four times, for this heartless act, No pity in his heart, that's a matter of fact."
Nathan pointed to David, "You are the man," he said, "Yahweh's words to you, listen and dread. I made you king, took you from Saul's hand, Gave you your master's house, and all the land."

"Yet you struck down Uriah, took his wife as your own, Evil in Yahweh's sight, now seeds of trouble are sown. The sword won’t leave your house, for the wrongs you've done, Your wives given to your neighbor, in the sight of the sun."
David confessed, "I have sinned against Yahweh's name," Nathan replied, "Your sin’s put away, but sorrow still came. The child shall die, for bringing shame to Yahweh's fame."

David mourned and fasted, pleading on the ground, But on the seventh day, silence was the sound. His servants feared the truth, their whispers caught his ear, "Is the child dead?" David asked, his voice sincere.

"He is dead," they replied, sorrow in their tone, David rose, washed, worshiped, on Yahweh’s throne. He ate and explained, "Who knows if grace would save, But now he’s gone, I shall join him in the grave."
Comforted Bathsheba, and they bore a son, Named Solomon, Yahweh's love to him was won. Nathan came again, and Jedidiah was his name, For Yahweh's sake, a child of great fame.
Meanwhile, Joab fought and Rabbah fell, He sent for David, with victories to tell. David gathered troops, took the city’s crown, Placed it on his head, wore Ammon’s renown.
He brought back the spoils, and with justice it was done, Returned to Jerusalem, battles won. David’s story marked by sorrow and fight, A tale of power, repentance, and the quest for what's right.
In the house of David, tension's brewing in the air, Absalom had a sis, Tamar, beauty rare. Amnon, her half-brother, loved her deep and true, But the love made him sick, didn't know what to do.
His friend Jonadab, sly and wise with a plan, Asked, "Why so sad, son of the king, my man?" Amnon confessed, "I love Tamar, Absalom's kin," Jonadab said, "Here's how you draw her in."
"Lie down, act sick, let the king come and see, Ask for Tamar to bake you some food personally." Amnon played his part, the king was deceived, Tamar came to bake, and Amnon's plot achieved.
She kneaded the dough, made cakes with grace, But Amnon had plans that would bring disgrace. He sent the others out, asked her to stay, But when he spoke his mind, Tamar said, "No way!"
"Don't force me, brother, this shouldn't be, Talk to the king, he'll not withhold me," she plea. But Amnon ignored, his strength he abused, A tragic act, Tamar was bruised.
After his crime, his love turned to hate, He threw her out, sealing her tragic fate. Tamar tore her robe, ashes on her head, With anguish and sorrow, her tears she shed.
Absalom saw her pain, his anger grew, But told her, "Sister, hold your peace, let it stew." King David heard, his anger burned, But silent he stayed, no justice discerned.
Two years passed, Absalom plotted his scheme, Invited all David's sons to a sheep-shearing scene. He asked the king to let Amnon attend, Pressing for a chance to bring Amnon's end.
Absalom's men struck when Amnon's heart was merry, The king's sons fled, the news they did carry. David mourned, his garments torn in despair, But Jonadab assured him, only Amnon's not there.

Absalom fled to Geshur, seeking refuge and space, While David longed for him, in a sorrowful embrace. Three years passed, David's heart began to mend, His grief for Amnon faded, but his longing for Absalom never did end.
Joab saw the king's heart was on Absalom's track, He sent for a wise woman, to bring his son back.
"Act like you're mourning," he whispered low, "Put on your mourning clothes, and let no oil flow."
She went to the king, fell face to the floor, "Help me, O king!" she cried, wanting more.
"What ails you?" he asked, with a curious eye, "I'm a widow," she said, "my husband's gone by."
"I had two sons; in the field, they fought, One struck the other, and now he's caught."
"The family wants blood, to kill the heir too, Quench my last coal, and what will I do?"
The king said, "Go home; I'll give a command, No one will bother, just understand."
She pleaded, "O king, let guilt be on me, Don't let the avenger my son seize."
"Not one hair will fall," he swore with might, The woman then paused, ready to ignite.
"Why don't you bring home your own son, banished away? We die, like spilled water, at the end of the day."
The king caught the scheme, asked if Joab's hand, The woman replied, "Your wisdom is grand."
So Joab was called, and the king decreed, "Bring Absalom back, fulfill the need."
Joab bowed low, his thankfulness clear, Absalom returned, but kept the king's face near.
Handsome Absalom, praised in the land, Cut his hair yearly, and grew as planned.
Two years passed in a distant space, Still, Absalom did not see the king's face.
He called Joab, twice with no heed, Set Joab's field ablaze, pushing his need.
Joab confronted, "Why burn my field's share?" Absalom spoke out, "I want to clear the air."
"Let me speak to the king, or let my life cease," Joab took his word, sought the king's peace.
Absalom bowed as he entered the room, The king kissed his son, resolving the gloom.
Absalom set the scene with horses and a ride, Fifty men running, showing his pride.
At the gate early, he'd stand and wait, Catching those seeking judgment from the king's estate.
"What city you from?" he'd call out loud, The men replied, feeling proud.
Said Absalom, "Your case is right, But no one's here from the king tonight."
He'd add, "If I were judge, I'd hear your plea, Justice and fairness, you'd get from me."
When folks bowed down, he'd pull them near, With a kiss and a smile, he'd steal their cheer.
He charmed all Israel, their hearts he won, Turning their loyalty, one by one.
Forty years later, he asked the king, "Let me go to Hebron, my vow to bring."
The king said, "Go in peace," so off he went, But spies he sent, with secret intent.
“When the trumpet sounds, say this thing, ‘Absalom in Hebron, is now the king!’”
Two hundred men in innocence came along, Unaware of the plan, they did no wrong.
He called Ahithophel, wise and sly, The conspiracy grew, reaching the sky.
A messenger came, “Absalom’s the one, The hearts of Israel, he has won.”
David rose, with urgency in his tone, “Let’s flee now, or lose the throne.”
The servants pledged their loyalty true, Ready for whatever David would do.
The king left ten to guard his place, Then departed with dignity, yet in haste.
David's crew moved on, loyal and tight, From Gath, six hundred, ready to fight.
Ittai the Gittite, David tried to send back, But Ittai swore loyalty, ready to attack.
"Where you go, I'll be," Ittai vowed, In life or death, standing proud.
They crossed the brook with tears and cries, Leaving Jerusalem under clouded skies.
Zadok came with the ark in tow, But David sent it back, trusting God’s flow.
“If God’s with me, I’ll return again, If not, let Him choose my end and reign.”
“Zadok, take peace, go back to the land, With your sons, keep me in command.”
David climbed Olives, weeping, head low, Barefoot, mourning, with sorrow in tow.
News reached him of betrayal deep, “Yahweh, make Ahithophel’s counsel cheap.”
Hushai met him, a friend in despair, David gave a mission, with care.
“Go back and serve; to Absalom speak, Defeat Ahithophel, make him weak.”
With Zadok and Abiathar near, Listen in secret, bring word clear.”
Hushai returned, the plan in place, While Absalom came, seeking his space.
